Liverpool John Lennon Airport is about a 25 to 35 minute drive or bus ride from the centre and focuses on UK and European budget routes; for long-haul you will usually use Manchester, under an hour away by train. You do not need a car to live here, and central parking and traffic make one more hassle than help for everyday nomad life.
liverpool.visas: The UK has no digital nomad visa. Visitors from the US, EU, Canada, Australia and many other countries can enter visa-free as standard visitors for up to six months, while others apply for a standard visitor visa; from 2025 many visa-exempt travellers also need an ETA (electronic travel authorisation) obtained in advance. Crucially, UK visitor rules were updated to permit remote working: you may carry out your normal job for an employer based outside the UK while visiting, provided remote work is not the main purpose of your trip. What you cannot do is work for a UK company, take up UK employment, or provide services to UK-based clients as if in the local labour market. There is no route to extend a visit into long-term residence on this basis. Rules evolve, so confirm current ETA and visitor conditions on the official UK government website before you travel.
liverpool.bestTime: Liverpool has a mild, damp maritime climate with no real extremes, so you trade cold winters for a lot of grey, wet days. The best window is May through September, when days are longest, temperatures are pleasantly warm rather than hot, and the waterfront, parks and outdoor events come alive; June to August is the reliable peak. Spring and early autumn are decent too, though changeable. Winter, from November through February, is not bitterly cold but is dark, wet and windy, with short daylight and frequent rain blowing in off the Irish Sea, which some find flattening over time. Rain is possible in any month, so a waterproof is essential year-round. If you dislike gloom, avoid the deep winter and aim for late spring to early autumn. There is no snowy-city drama here, just the classic UK pattern of mild, damp and often overcast.
liverpool.prosCons: Pros: Liverpool offers genuine character, a famous music and football culture, a striking UNESCO-linked waterfront and a warm, sociable local scene, all at rents well below London. It is compact, walkable, English-speaking and well connected by rail, with a creative coworking hub in the Baltic Triangle and a big student population that keeps nightlife and cafes buzzing and affordable. Cons: the weather is often grey, wet and windy, especially in winter, and the short daylight can wear on you. As a regional city it lacks London's scale of international flights and the very largest nomad community, and you will route long-haul trips through Manchester. Some areas feel rough around the edges, and match days and stag or hen crowds can make the centre rowdy. For value, friendliness and culture it punches well above its size, but do not expect sunshine or a huge global-nomad scene.
liverpool.whoFor: Liverpool suits budget-conscious nomads who want an affordable, characterful UK base with genuine warmth, music and football culture, and an easygoing, sociable atmosphere. It is a strong fit if you value a walkable, English-speaking city with a real creative community and good rail links over polish or prestige, and it works well for solo remote workers thanks to the lively cafe and coworking scene in the Baltic Triangle and a large, friendly student crowd. Football and music fans will feel especially at home. It is less ideal if you need reliable sunshine, a huge international nomad hub or frequent direct long-haul flights, since those mean leaning on Manchester and enduring a lot of grey, damp weather. Come for value, culture and a welcoming vibe; look elsewhere if warmth and a big global scene are your priorities.

cardiff.costOfLiving: Cardiff, the Welsh capital, is reasonably priced for a UK capital city, and these are editorial estimates in USD. A one-bedroom flat in or near the centre (Cardiff Bay, Cathays, the city core) runs roughly $950 to $1,200 a month, easing to around $750 to $950 in areas further out like Roath or Canton. Groceries for one come to about $300, with a casual meal out around $15 to $22 and a pint near $5 to $6. A monthly bus and local rail pass is roughly $75 to $90. A coworking hot desk sits near $150 to $220. Add utilities, phone and any council tax on a longer let, and a comfortable solo month lands close to $2,300. Cardiff is cheaper than London and comparable to other UK regional cities, and staying central lets you live easily without a car.
cardiff.whereToWork: Cardiff has a solid coworking and cafe-work scene for its size, with flexible desks and private offices around the city centre and Cardiff Bay, and a growing cluster of creative and tech spaces serving the capital's media and digital sector. Home broadband and wifi are reliable, with fibre widely available and good speeds across the centre. Cafe culture is comfortable for laptop work: independent coffee shops in Cathays, Roath and the arcades of the historic centre are used to remote workers, and the compact centre makes hopping between them easy. English is universal; Welsh is also an official language and visible on signage, but you will never need it to work or live. A large student population keeps casual workspaces busy and affordable. The main caveats are that popular cafes fill during term time, and options, while good, are fewer than in a larger metropolis.
cardiff.gettingAround: Cardiff is compact, flat and very walkable, and you can cover the centre, Cardiff Bay and the main residential areas easily on foot or by bike. Public transport is good: frequent local buses plus Valley Lines trains connect the centre with the bay and the wider region, and a monthly pass runs roughly $75 to $90. Uber and traditional taxis both operate. Cardiff Airport is about 12 miles west of the city, a 30 to 40 minute drive or a bus and train combination, and mainly serves a limited set of UK and European routes; for wider choice, many travellers use Bristol Airport across the border or take the fast train to London for long-haul from Heathrow. You do not need a car to live in Cardiff, and the walkable core plus decent transit make one more of a burden than a help for everyday life.
cardiff.visas: The UK has no digital nomad visa, and Cardiff follows the same national rules as the rest of the UK, including Wales. Visitors from the US, EU, Canada, Australia and many other countries can enter visa-free as standard visitors for up to six months, while others need a standard visitor visa; many visa-exempt travellers now also require an ETA (electronic travel authorisation) arranged in advance. UK rules permit remote working as a visitor: you may do your normal job for an employer based outside the UK while here, as long as that remote work is not the primary reason for your trip. You cannot work for a UK company, take UK employment or serve UK-based clients as part of the local labour market, and visitor status offers no path to long-term residence. Confirm current ETA and visitor conditions on the official UK government website before you travel, as requirements change.
cardiff.bestTime: Cardiff has a mild, wet maritime climate, and coastal Wales is genuinely one of the rainier corners of the UK, so a waterproof is a year-round essential. The best months are May through September, when daylight is long, temperatures are pleasantly warm without being hot, and the parks, bay and outdoor events are at their best; June to August is the reliable peak, though showers still interrupt. Spring and early autumn are pleasant but changeable. Winter, from November to February, is not severely cold but is dark, grey, windy and often persistently wet, with short daylight that can feel draining over weeks. Rain can arrive in any season and any month, so plan around it rather than expecting to avoid it. If you dislike damp gloom, target late spring through early autumn. There is little snow, just the familiar mild, overcast and often soggy UK pattern.
cardiff.prosCons: Pros: Cardiff is a friendly, compact and affordable capital with a walkable, flat centre, a revitalised waterfront at Cardiff Bay, a strong sporting culture and quick access to spectacular Welsh coast and countryside, including the Brecon Beacons. It is English-speaking, cheaper than London, well served by trains, and has a lively student-fuelled cafe and nightlife scene plus a growing creative and media sector. Cons: the weather is notably wet even by UK standards, and winters are dark, grey and damp. As a smaller capital, its airport is limited, so wider travel often means using Bristol or heading to London, and the international nomad community is modest. Nightlife around the centre can get rowdy on weekends and match or rugby days. For value, friendliness and easy access to nature it is excellent, but do not come expecting sunshine or a large global-nomad hub.
cardiff.whoFor: Cardiff suits nomads who want an affordable, walkable, English-speaking UK capital with a relaxed, friendly feel and outstanding access to nature, from the Welsh coast to the mountains of the Brecon Beacons, all within easy reach. It is a strong fit for outdoors lovers, sports and rugby fans, and anyone who prefers a compact, manageable city over a sprawling metropolis, with a lively student scene keeping cafes and coworking affordable and sociable. Solo remote workers will find it easy to settle into and get around. It is less ideal if you need reliable sunshine, a large international nomad community or a major long-haul airport, since Cardiff's weather is decidedly wet and wider travel leans on Bristol or London. Come for value, warmth of welcome and quick escapes into some of Britain's best scenery; look elsewhere if you crave sun or a big global scene.

belfast.costOfLiving: Belfast is among the most affordable cities in the UK, and these are editorial estimates in USD. A one-bedroom flat in or near the centre (the Cathedral Quarter, city core, Queen's Quarter) runs roughly $800 to $1,050 a month, dropping to around $650 to $850 further out. Groceries for one come to about $290, with a casual meal out around $14 to $20 and a pint near $5. Public transport is inexpensive, with a monthly bus and Glider pass roughly $60 to $80. A coworking hot desk sits near $130 to $200. Add utilities, phone and any rates or council charges on a longer let, and a comfortable solo month lands close to $2,100, making Belfast noticeably cheaper than most of mainland Britain. Living centrally keeps you car-free and easily walkable, and the low rents are the city's standout value for nomads.
belfast.whereToWork: Belfast has a surprisingly strong coworking and tech scene for its size, driven by a booming cybersecurity, fintech and creative sector, with flexible desks and offices clustered around the Cathedral Quarter and city centre. Home broadband is excellent: Northern Ireland has some of the best full-fibre coverage in the UK, so fast, reliable connections are easy to secure. Cafe-work culture is comfortable and welcoming, with independent coffee shops in the Cathedral Quarter, around Queen's University and in the city centre used to laptop workers, and the compact core makes moving between them simple. English is universal. The large student population and growing pool of remote workers and founders keep casual workspaces busy and affordable, and there is a genuine, tight-knit community feel. Caveats are minor: the overall scene is smaller than in a big metro, and popular cafes can fill during term time, but for its size Belfast punches well above its weight.
belfast.gettingAround: Belfast is compact, flat and very walkable, and you can cover the centre, the Cathedral Quarter and the university area comfortably on foot. Public transport is straightforward: local buses plus the Glider rapid-transit service link key routes across the city, and a monthly pass runs roughly $60 to $80. Uber operates alongside traditional taxis, which are plentiful. There are two airports: George Best Belfast City Airport sits just a few minutes from the centre and handles mainly UK and Ireland routes, while Belfast International, about 30 minutes out, adds more European and budget options; for long-haul you will often connect via Dublin, London or Manchester. Dublin is also reachable by direct train in around two hours. You do not need a car to live in Belfast, though one helps for exploring the Antrim coast, the Giant's Causeway and the wider countryside at your own pace.
belfast.visas: The UK has no digital nomad visa, and Belfast, as part of Northern Ireland, follows the same UK-wide rules. Visitors from the US, EU, Canada, Australia and many other countries can enter visa-free as standard visitors for up to six months, while others need a standard visitor visa; many visa-exempt travellers now also require an ETA (electronic travel authorisation) obtained in advance. UK rules allow remote working as a visitor: you may perform your normal job for an employer based outside the UK while here, provided that remote work is not the main purpose of your trip. You cannot work for a UK company, take UK employment or serve UK-based clients within the local labour market, and there is no route from a visit to long-term residence. Note that crossing into the neighbouring Republic of Ireland is a separate jurisdiction with its own rules. Always confirm current ETA and visitor conditions on the official UK government website before travelling.
belfast.bestTime: Belfast has a mild, wet maritime climate with cool summers and soft, rarely freezing winters, so the trade-off is a great deal of grey and rain rather than extreme cold. The best months are May through September, when daylight stretches long, temperatures are comfortably mild, and the city and nearby Antrim coast are at their most inviting; June to August is the reliable peak, though showers still punctuate most weeks. Spring and early autumn are pleasant but changeable. Winter, from November to February, is dark, damp and windy, with short daylight and frequent rain rolling in off the Atlantic, which can feel wearing over time even though it rarely gets truly cold or snowy. Rain is possible in any month, so a waterproof is essential year-round. If you dislike gloom and damp, aim for late spring through early autumn and treat any dry spell as a bonus.
belfast.prosCons: Pros: Belfast is one of the UK's best-value cities, with low rents, cheap daily costs and excellent full-fibre internet, plus a fast-growing tech and creative scene and a genuinely warm, community-minded local feel. It is compact, walkable and English-speaking, with easy access to the stunning Antrim coast and the Giant's Causeway, and Dublin only a short train away. The cafe and coworking scene is lively for its size. Cons: the weather is often grey, damp and windy, and winters are dark with limited daylight. It is a small city, so nightlife, the international nomad community and long-haul flights are limited, and wider travel usually routes through Dublin, London or Manchester. Some visitors are conscious of the city's history and divided areas, though the centre is safe and welcoming. For value, connectivity and access to dramatic coastline it is excellent, if short on sun and scale.
belfast.whoFor: Belfast suits budget-focused nomads who want maximum value in the UK without sacrificing fast internet, safety or a walkable, English-speaking city with real character. It is a strong fit for tech workers and founders drawn to a growing cybersecurity and fintech scene, and for anyone who prefers a compact, friendly, community-oriented base over a large impersonal metropolis. Outdoors lovers will prize the quick access to the Antrim coast, the Giant's Causeway and the northern Irish countryside, and Dublin sits within an easy train ride for a change of pace. It works well for solo remote workers thanks to the affordable cafe and coworking scene and a large student presence. It is less ideal if you need dependable sunshine, a big international nomad hub or frequent direct long-haul flights, since the weather is wet and wider travel leans on Dublin or larger UK airports. Come for value and welcome.

leeds.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200/month as a solo remote worker (editorial estimates, converted to USD). A one-bed flat in the city centre runs roughly $1,150-1,400, while something a mile or two out (Headingley, Hyde Park, Kirkstall) drops to $850-1,050. Groceries land near $300-380 if you cook most meals; a supermarket meal deal is about $5. Eating out is the swing factor: a casual pub lunch is $14-18, a mid-range dinner for one $28-40, a flat white $4. A monthly bus pass is roughly $80, and most centre living is walkable so many skip transport entirely. Hot-desk coworking memberships sit around $180-260/month. Utilities and broadband add $180-230 in a one-bed. Leeds is noticeably cheaper than London for similar city amenities, but energy bills and rent have both climbed in recent years.
leeds.whereToWork: Leeds has a solid coworking scene clustered around the city centre and the South Bank regeneration zone, with hot-desks broadly $180-260/month and day passes around $20-30. Central Leeds and the university district have dense, reliable fibre broadband, and public wifi in libraries and larger cafes is generally dependable. As a UK city there is no firewall or VPN requirement, so Google, WhatsApp, and Western services all work normally on both wifi and 4G/5G. Mobile data is cheap and widely available; unlimited SIM plans run roughly $16-26/month. Cafe-work culture is strong, especially in independent spots around Call Lane, Chapel Allerton, and Headingley, though some busier chains discourage all-day laptop camping at peak times. Trinity Leeds and the Corn Exchange add sheltered spots with power. For quiet focus, the central library reading rooms are a reliable free option.
leeds.gettingAround: Leeds is compact and very walkable; most of the centre is covered on foot in 20-25 minutes. It is one of the largest UK cities without a metro or tram, so buses do the heavy lifting, backed by a busy rail station with fast links to Manchester, York, and London (roughly two hours to the capital). Buses are frequent in the core but can be slow and patchy to outer suburbs, and a single fare is capped at around $3.50. Ride-hailing via Uber and local firms is easy and affordable, with short city hops about $8-13. Leeds Bradford Airport sits northwest of the city with mostly European and domestic routes; Manchester Airport, under an hour by train, covers long-haul. You do not need a car to live centrally, and parking is pricey, though a car helps for exploring the Yorkshire Dales and coast on weekends.
leeds.visas: The UK has no dedicated digital nomad visa. Many nationalities (including US, EU, Canadian, Australian, and Japanese passport holders) can enter as a visitor without applying in advance and stay up to six months; others must obtain a Standard Visitor visa beforehand. Under current Home Office guidance, visitors are generally permitted to do remote work for an employer or clients based outside the UK incidentally during their stay, but you cannot take UK employment, fill a role in the UK labour market, or run a business serving UK clients. The visitor route is not designed for indefinite living, and repeated back-to-back stays can draw scrutiny at the border. Note the UK now also requires an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) for many visa-exempt visitors. Rules change frequently, so verify your nationality's current requirements on the official GOV.UK site before booking travel.
leeds.bestTime: Leeds has a cool, temperate maritime climate with no extremes but plenty of grey. The best stretch is late May through early September, when days are long (light past 9pm in June) and highs sit around 66-70F, ideal for the parks, canal walks, and nearby Dales. Summer sees the liveliest festivals and outdoor markets, though rain is possible any month, so pack layers and a waterproof regardless of season. Spring (April-May) is pleasant and quieter. Autumn brings crisp, atmospheric days but shortening light. Winter (December-February) is the trade-off: damp, overcast, and dark by mid-afternoon, with highs near 43F and occasional frost or light snow rather than deep cold. It rarely gets punishingly cold, but the persistent gloom is the main thing to brace for. If daylight and mood matter to you, aim for the June-August window.
leeds.prosCons: Pros: Leeds is a genuinely affordable major UK city compared with London, with a big-city feel at a fraction of the cost. It has a lively independent food, music, and nightlife scene, a large student and young-professional population, strong rail links across the north, and the Yorkshire Dales and coast within easy reach. English-speaking, safe by UK standards, and walkable in the core. Cons: the weather is frequently grey and wet with short winter days that wear on some people. There is no metro or tram, so outer-area transit leans on sometimes-unreliable buses. The airport is small with limited long-haul, meaning a Manchester detour for many flights. Rents and energy bills have risen sharply, denting the affordability edge, and like much of the UK, some high-street areas feel tired. It lacks the international nomad density of London or Lisbon.
leeds.whoFor: Leeds suits the remote worker who wants a real, functioning UK city without London prices or intensity. It is a strong fit if you value a walkable centre, a warm and unpretentious social scene, good live music and independent food, and quick weekend escapes into classic Yorkshire countryside. English-speaking convenience and general safety make it low-friction for first-time UK stays or those on a working-holiday. It works well for solo nomads and couples who prefer a mid-sized, sociable base over a tourist hotspot, and for anyone with UK or European clients wanting a central-northern hub with fast trains. It is less ideal if you need year-round sunshine, a large established international nomad community, frequent long-haul flights from your doorstep, or a metro system. Budget-conscious professionals, students, and creatives tend to click with Leeds fastest.

chengdu.costOfLiving: Plan on roughly $1,200/month as a solo remote worker (editorial estimates in USD, converted from RMB). A modern one-bed in a central district like Jinjiang or Wuhou runs about $400-550, dropping to $260-380 a few metro stops out. Chengdu is famously relaxed and cheap: a bowl of noodles or a street breakfast is $1.50-3, and a full hotpot feast with friends lands around $12-18 a head. Cooking from wet markets and supermarkets keeps groceries near $180-250. The metro is astonishingly cheap at roughly $0.30-0.85 a ride, so monthly transport rarely tops $30. Coworking hot-desks run about $90-150/month, though many nomads work from the city's dense cafe scene for the price of a $4 coffee. Utilities and fast fibre broadband add $40-70. Overall, Chengdu delivers a big-city lifestyle at a genuinely low cost, with food quality far above what the price suggests.
chengdu.whereToWork: Chengdu has a growing coworking scene, with hot-desks broadly $90-150/month concentrated in the central and high-tech (Tianfu) districts, plus plentiful cafes that tolerate all-day laptop work. Fibre broadband and 5G are fast and reliable, and mobile data is cheap and abundant. The critical caveat is the Great Firewall: Google, Gmail, WhatsApp, Instagram, and many Western sites are blocked, so you must install and test a reputable VPN before you arrive, since VPN sites themselves are hard to reach once you are in-country. Have a backup VPN too, as reliability fluctuates. Chinese super-apps (WeChat, Alipay) run everything from payments to taxis, so set those up early. Cafe-work culture is strong and social; independent coffee shops in Jinjiang and around the universities are welcoming to remote workers. Coworking staff rarely speak much English, so translation apps help. For video calls, always confirm your VPN is stable first.
chengdu.gettingAround: Chengdu has one of China's best and cheapest metro systems, with a dozen-plus lines, clean modern trains, and fares around $0.30-0.85 that reach almost everywhere you would want to go, including both airports. The city is broadly flat and increasingly walkable in central districts, though it sprawls, so combine walking with the metro. Didi (China's Uber) is ubiquitous, easy to use through WeChat or Alipay once linked, and cheap: cross-town rides are often $3-7. You do not need a car. Bike-share is everywhere for short hops. Chengdu Tianfu International Airport (opened 2021) handles growing international routes, while the older Shuangliu Airport covers domestic and regional flights; both connect by metro or a short Didi. High-speed rail links Chengdu to Chongqing, Xian, and beyond in a few hours. Between the metro, Didi, and bikes, getting around is one of the easiest and cheapest parts of Chengdu life.
chengdu.visas: China has significantly expanded visa-free access in 2024-2025, granting unilateral visa-free entry of up to 30 days to passport holders from many countries, including much of the EU, plus Australia, New Zealand, Japan, and others; the list keeps growing, so check whether yours is included. Separately, a transit visa-free policy now allows eligible travelers from many nationalities to stay up to 240 hours (10 days) when passing through to a third country, and Chengdu is a covered entry point. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa, and technically these entries are for tourism, business, or transit rather than employment, so working remotely for a foreign employer sits in a grey area travelers should be discreet about. For longer stays you would need a proper visa (M, F, or similar) arranged in advance. Rules shift frequently, so verify your nationality's current eligibility and permitted duration on official Chinese government or embassy sources before traveling.
chengdu.bestTime: Chengdu sits in a humid subtropical basin known for grey, overcast skies and relatively little direct sun year-round. The best windows are spring (March-May) and autumn (September-November), when temperatures are mild, roughly 60-77F, and the humidity is more bearable. Summers (June-August) are hot, sticky, and humid with highs in the upper 80s to low 90s F and frequent rain, though the basin traps haze and it rarely feels crisp. Winters (December-February) are not freezing but are damp, chilly, and famously gloomy, with highs around 50F and persistent cloud that many find dreary; buildings often lack good heating. If clear skies and comfort matter, target April, May, October, or early November. Whatever the season, expect more cloud than sun; Chengdu is not a place you come for bright weather, but the mild temperatures and lush greenery make spring and autumn genuinely pleasant.
chengdu.prosCons: Pros: Chengdu is cheap, safe, and famously laid-back, with a slower pace than Beijing or Shanghai. The food, especially Sichuan hotpot and street snacks, is world-class and inexpensive. The metro is superb and dirt-cheap, ride-hailing is easy, and there is a real cafe and teahouse culture, plus pandas and nearby mountains for weekends. A growing expat and creative scene helps. Cons: the Great Firewall means a VPN is essential for Google, WhatsApp, and most Western sites, and it is not always reliable. The language barrier is significant, with limited English outside tourist and tech circles, so translation apps and WeChat/Alipay setup are must-dos. The weather is often grey and humid with little sun, winters are damp and cold indoors, and air quality can dip. Payments and daily life run entirely on Chinese apps, which takes adjustment. Bureaucracy and long-stay visas remain awkward.
chengdu.whoFor: Chengdu suits the adventurous, budget-conscious nomad who wants an authentic, deeply local Chinese experience rather than a polished expat bubble. It is ideal if you love food above almost everything, appreciate a relaxed pace, and are comfortable navigating a real language barrier with translation apps and patience. The low cost and excellent transit make it great for stretching a modest income while living well, and the cafe and teahouse culture rewards those happy to work socially in public. It fits solo travelers, foodies, and the culturally curious who see the VPN and app setup as a solvable hurdle rather than a dealbreaker. It is less suited to anyone who needs seamless access to Western services, a large English-speaking community, reliable sunshine, or an easy long-term visa path. Come for the food, the value, and the mellow vibe; stay flexible on connectivity and communication.

xian.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100/month as a solo remote worker in Xian (editorial estimates in USD, converted from RMB), making it one of China's more affordable major cities. A one-bed apartment near the centre inside or close to the ancient city walls runs about $350-480, dropping to $230-330 in outer districts a short metro ride away. Food is a highlight and a bargain: a famous roujiamo (meat sandwich) or bowl of biangbiang noodles is $1.50-3, and a hearty Muslim Quarter feast for one lands under $8. Home cooking from local markets keeps groceries near $160-230. The metro costs roughly $0.30-0.75 a ride, so transport rarely exceeds $25/month. Coworking hot-desks run about $80-130/month, though many work from cafes for a $3-4 coffee. Utilities and fast broadband add $40-65. Xian delivers rich history and excellent food at a noticeably lower cost than the eastern coastal megacities.
xian.whereToWork: Xian's coworking scene is smaller than Chengdu's or Shanghai's but functional, with hot-desks broadly $80-130/month clustered in the high-tech zone and near the universities in the south of the city. Fibre broadband and 5G are fast and cheap, and mobile data is plentiful. As everywhere in mainland China, the Great Firewall blocks Google, Gmail, WhatsApp, Instagram, and many Western sites, so install and test a reliable VPN before you arrive, keep a backup, and expect occasional instability during video calls. Set up WeChat and Alipay early, since daily life and payments run on them. Cafe-work culture is present, with a decent independent coffee scene in the university districts and the trendier areas near the walls, though staff rarely speak much English, so translation apps are essential. Xian sees fewer foreign remote workers than the coastal hubs, so expect a more local, less English-friendly environment. Always confirm your VPN before scheduling meetings.
xian.gettingAround: Xian has an excellent, cheap, and expanding metro system, with modern trains and fares around $0.30-0.75 that connect the walled centre, the high-speed rail station, and the airport line. The historic core inside the Ming-era city walls is compact and walkable, and you can even cycle the top of the walls themselves. Beyond the centre the city sprawls, so the metro plus Didi (China's Uber) covers the gaps; Didi is easy once linked to WeChat or Alipay, with typical rides $3-6. Bike-share handles short hops. You do not need a car. Xianyang International Airport, northwest of the city, is well connected by a dedicated metro line and airport buses and handles growing domestic and some international routes. High-speed rail links Xian to Chengdu, Beijing, and Luoyang in a few hours. The Terracotta Army is reachable by public bus or Didi. Between metro, Didi, and bikes, getting around is cheap and straightforward.
xian.visas: China expanded visa-free access substantially in 2024-2025, offering unilateral visa-free entry of up to 30 days to passport holders from many countries, including much of the EU plus Australia, New Zealand, Japan, and others; confirm whether your nationality is currently on the list, as it keeps changing. A separate transit visa-free policy allows eligible travelers to stay up to 240 hours (10 days) when transiting to a third country, and Xian is among the covered entry points. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa, and these entries are officially for tourism, business, or transit rather than employment, so remote work for a foreign employer occupies a grey area best kept low-profile. Longer stays require a proper visa (such as M or F) arranged in advance through a Chinese embassy or consulate. Because eligibility, durations, and covered ports of entry change frequently, always verify the current rules for your passport on official Chinese government sources before you travel.
xian.bestTime: Xian has a temperate continental climate with four distinct seasons, more variation than the humid southern cities. The best times to visit are spring (April-May) and autumn (September-October), when days are mild and dry, roughly 60-77F, with clearer skies and comfortable sightseeing weather for the walls and Terracotta Army. Summers (June-August) are hot and can be humid, with highs in the upper 80s to mid-90s F and occasional heavy rain, plus dusty haze. Winters (December-February) are cold and dry, with highs near 40F, freezing nights, and some of China's worst seasonal air pollution as coal heating and the sheltered basin location trap smog; this is the main season to avoid if air quality concerns you. Spring can bring occasional dust from the north. Overall, aim for the April-May or September-October shoulder windows for the most pleasant temperatures and the cleanest air.
xian.prosCons: Pros: Xian is affordable even by Chinese standards, safe, and steeped in history as an ancient capital, with the Terracotta Army, intact city walls, and the atmospheric Muslim Quarter on your doorstep. The food is outstanding and cheap, blending Shaanxi and Silk Road flavours. The metro is excellent and inexpensive, ride-hailing is easy, and high-speed rail connects you across the country. It offers a deeply local Chinese experience at low cost. Cons: the Great Firewall makes a reliable VPN mandatory for Western services, and English is spoken far less than in coastal hubs, so the language barrier is real. Winter air pollution can be severe, and winters are cold with poor indoor heating in some buildings. The foreign nomad community is small, daily life runs entirely on Chinese apps, and long-term visas remain difficult. Summers are hot and hazy. It is more historic than cosmopolitan.
xian.whoFor: Xian suits the history-loving, budget-focused nomad who wants an authentic inland Chinese base rather than a glossy coastal expat scene. It is ideal if you are fascinated by ancient China, enjoy exploring imperial sites and Silk Road culture on your doorstep, and see hearty Shaanxi food as a daily draw. The rock-bottom cost of living lets a modest income go a long way, and the excellent metro and rail links make it a comfortable hub for exploring central China. It fits independent, culturally curious travelers who are comfortable with a significant language barrier and treat the VPN and app setup as routine. It is a poor fit for anyone needing a large English-speaking community, seamless Western connectivity, clean winter air, or an easy long-stay visa. Come to Xian for history, food, and value; be ready for a very local, less international day-to-day experience.

hangzhou.costOfLiving: Expect roughly $1,400/month as a solo remote worker in Hangzhou (editorial estimates in USD, converted from RMB). As a prosperous tech city, it costs more than inland hubs like Chengdu or Xian but stays cheaper than Shanghai. A one-bed apartment in a central district near West Lake runs about $500-700, dropping to $330-480 further out along a metro line. Food spans cheap to refined: a noodle or dumpling meal is $2-4, while a mid-range restaurant dinner for one is $10-16. Cooking from local markets keeps groceries near $200-280. The excellent metro costs about $0.30-0.85 a ride, so transport rarely tops $30/month. Coworking hot-desks run around $110-180/month, reflecting the city's strong startup scene, though cafes are a popular free-ish alternative for a $4-5 coffee. Utilities and fast fibre add $50-75. Hangzhou offers a high quality of life and scenic surroundings at a mid-tier Chinese price.
hangzhou.whereToWork: Hangzhou is a genuine tech hub, home to Alibaba, so it has one of China's more developed coworking and startup ecosystems, with hot-desks broadly $110-180/month concentrated in the Binjiang, Future Sci-Tech City, and West Lake districts. Fibre broadband and 5G are fast and reliable, and mobile data is cheap and fast. The Great Firewall still applies: Google, Gmail, WhatsApp, Instagram, and many Western sites are blocked, so set up and test a solid VPN before arriving, keep a backup, and verify stability before video calls. WeChat and Alipay (the latter born in Hangzhou) run daily payments and services, so configure them early. Cafe-work culture is strong, with an abundant independent coffee scene around West Lake and the university areas, and the tech workforce means laptop-friendly venues are easy to find. English is more common here than in inland cities but still limited, so translation apps remain useful. The startup density makes networking and finding fellow remote workers easier.
hangzhou.gettingAround: Hangzhou has a modern, extensive, and cheap metro system, expanded significantly around the 2023 Asian Games, with fares around $0.30-0.85 that reach the airport, high-speed rail stations, and West Lake area. The lakeside districts are scenic and highly walkable, and cycling around West Lake is a pleasure, aided by ubiquitous bike-share. The city is large and sprawling, so the metro plus Didi (China's Uber) covers longer trips; Didi is easy once linked to WeChat or Alipay, with typical rides $3-7. You do not need a car. Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport handles extensive domestic and a good range of international flights and connects to the city by metro and airport buses. High-speed rail puts Shanghai under an hour away and Suzhou, Nanjing, and beyond within easy reach, making Hangzhou an excellent base for exploring the Yangtze Delta. Between metro, Didi, and bikes, daily mobility is cheap and efficient.
hangzhou.visas: China broadened visa-free access considerably in 2024-2025, granting unilateral visa-free entry of up to 30 days to passport holders from many countries, including much of the EU plus Australia, New Zealand, Japan, and more; check whether your nationality currently qualifies, as the list is frequently updated. A separate transit visa-free policy lets eligible travelers stay up to 240 hours (10 days) when transiting to a third country, and Hangzhou is a covered port of entry via its international airport. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa, and these entries are officially for tourism, business, or transit rather than employment, so remote work for an overseas employer sits in a grey area best handled discreetly. Longer stays require an appropriate visa (M, F, or similar) obtained in advance from a Chinese embassy or consulate. Since eligibility, permitted durations, and covered entry points change often, always confirm the current rules for your passport on official Chinese government sources before booking.
hangzhou.bestTime: Hangzhou has a humid subtropical climate with hot, sticky summers and cool, damp winters, so the shoulder seasons are clearly best. Aim for spring (late March-May), when West Lake is at its most beautiful with blossoms and mild 60-75F days, or autumn (late September-November), which brings crisp, clear, comfortable weather and the famous osmanthus blooms. Summers (June-August) are the season to avoid for comfort: high heat in the upper 80s to mid-90s F, oppressive humidity, and the June-July plum rains that bring long stretches of drizzle. Winters (December-February) are not severely cold but are chilly, grey, and damp, with highs around 46F and inadequate indoor heating in many buildings, making them feel colder than the numbers suggest. Occasional summer typhoon remnants can bring heavy rain. For the postcard version of Hangzhou and the most pleasant working weather, target April-May or October-November.
hangzhou.prosCons: Pros: Hangzhou pairs genuine natural beauty, West Lake and surrounding tea hills, with a modern, prosperous tech-city infrastructure. It is safe, has an excellent cheap metro, easy ride-hailing, and a strong startup and coworking scene thanks to Alibaba, plus slightly more English and a more developed cafe culture than inland cities. Shanghai is under an hour away by high-speed rail. Quality of life is high for the price. Cons: it costs more than inland Chinese hubs, though still below Shanghai. The Great Firewall means a VPN is essential for Western services and can be unreliable. Summers are hot and oppressively humid with a long rainy plum season, and winters are damp and poorly heated indoors. English is still limited outside tech and tourist circles, daily life runs on Chinese apps, and long-stay visas remain awkward. West Lake gets very crowded with domestic tourists on holidays.
hangzhou.whoFor: Hangzhou suits the nomad who wants natural beauty and a modern tech-city vibe without the full cost or intensity of Shanghai. It is ideal if you value scenic surroundings, West Lake, tea plantations, and cycling paths, alongside a real startup and coworking ecosystem that makes networking and finding fellow remote workers easier. The strong cafe culture, slightly better English, and fast rail link to Shanghai make it a comfortable, well-connected base for the Yangtze Delta. It fits professionals and entrepreneurs drawn to China's tech scene, couples wanting a livable and photogenic city, and those who want local authenticity with more polish than inland hubs offer. It is less ideal for anyone on a rock-bottom budget, those needing seamless Western connectivity, or people who wilt in humid subtropical summers. Come to Hangzhou for the blend of scenery, tech energy, and quality of life; budget a bit more and bring a reliable VPN.

guangzhou.costOfLiving: Plan on roughly $1,400/month as a solo remote worker in Guangzhou (editorial estimates in USD, converted from RMB), a major southern megacity cheaper than Shenzhen or Shanghai but pricier than inland hubs. A one-bed apartment in a central district like Tianhe or Yuexiu runs about $500-700, dropping to $330-480 further out along a metro line. Food is a defining draw: Cantonese cooking runs from $2-4 street bowls and morning dim sum to $12-18 mid-range dinners, and eating well cheaply is effortless. Cooking from the abundant wet markets keeps groceries near $200-280. The vast metro costs about $0.30-0.85 a ride, so transport rarely exceeds $30/month. Coworking hot-desks run around $110-170/month, with plenty of cafes as an alternative for a $4-5 coffee. Utilities, with heavy summer air-conditioning use, plus fast fibre add $55-85. Guangzhou delivers world-class food and full megacity infrastructure at a mid-tier Chinese cost.
guangzhou.whereToWork: Guangzhou, a huge commercial and trade hub, has a solid coworking scene with hot-desks broadly $110-170/month concentrated in the Tianhe CBD and Zhujiang New Town business districts, plus abundant cafes for laptop work. Fibre broadband and 5G are fast and reliable, and mobile data is cheap and abundant. The Great Firewall applies as everywhere in mainland China: Google, Gmail, WhatsApp, Instagram, and many Western sites are blocked, so install and test a dependable VPN before you arrive, keep a backup, and confirm stability before video calls. WeChat and Alipay run payments and daily life, so set them up early. Because Guangzhou hosts the huge Canton Fair and a large trading community, you will find pockets of English and international business services, more than in inland cities, though it is still limited outside those circles, so translation apps help. Cafe-work culture is well established across Tianhe and the university areas. Always verify your VPN before scheduling meetings.
guangzhou.gettingAround: Guangzhou has one of the world's largest and best metro systems, with many lines, modern trains, and fares around $0.30-0.85 that blanket the city and reach both the airport and the high-speed rail stations. The city is dense and generally walkable in central districts, though the summer heat and humidity often push you underground or into a Didi. Didi (China's Uber) is ubiquitous and cheap once linked to WeChat or Alipay, with typical rides $3-7. You do not need a car, and bike-share covers short hops. Baiyun International Airport, one of China's busiest, offers extensive domestic and international routes and connects to the centre by metro. High-speed rail links Guangzhou to Shenzhen and Hong Kong in about an hour and across the country in a few hours, making it a superb base for the Pearl River Delta. Between the sprawling metro, cheap Didi, and rail, getting around Guangzhou is efficient and inexpensive.
guangzhou.visas: China expanded visa-free access significantly in 2024-2025, granting unilateral visa-free entry of up to 30 days to passport holders from many countries, including much of the EU plus Australia, New Zealand, Japan, and others; verify whether your nationality currently qualifies, as the list is updated frequently. A separate transit visa-free policy allows eligible travelers to stay up to 240 hours (10 days) when transiting to a third country, and Guangzhou, with its major international airport and proximity to Hong Kong, is a well-used covered entry point. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa, and these entries are officially for tourism, business, or transit rather than employment, so remote work for a foreign employer sits in a grey area best kept discreet. Longer stays require a proper visa (M, F, or similar) arranged in advance through a Chinese embassy or consulate. Because eligibility, durations, and covered ports of entry change often, always confirm the current rules for your passport on official Chinese government sources before traveling.
guangzhou.bestTime: Guangzhou has a humid subtropical, almost tropical climate with long, intensely hot and sticky summers and short, mild winters, so timing matters a lot for comfort. The best window is autumn and early winter (late October-December), when the humidity finally eases and days are pleasant and dry, roughly 65-78F. Spring (March-April) is warm but often wet and grey with heavy humidity. The season to avoid is the long summer from May through September: high heat in the upper 80s to mid-90s F, oppressive humidity, frequent heavy downpours, and typhoon season, which can bring storms and travel disruption from the South China Sea. Winters (January-February) are short and mild with highs around 65F, occasionally cool and damp but rarely cold, and no snow. If you can only come once, aim for November or December for the most comfortable, driest, and most reliably pleasant working weather in Guangzhou.
guangzhou.prosCons: Pros: Guangzhou is a full-service megacity with arguably China's best food, the home of Cantonese cuisine and dim sum, at a mid-tier cost. It has an enormous, cheap, world-class metro, easy ride-hailing, a busy international airport, and fast rail to Shenzhen and Hong Kong. As a major trade hub it has more English and international business infrastructure than inland cities, and it is safe with a warm southern energy. Cons: the climate is punishing, with long, oppressively hot and humid summers and a real typhoon season. The Great Firewall makes a reliable VPN essential for Western services. It is a sprawling, dense, sometimes gritty industrial-commercial city with fewer marquee scenic draws than Hangzhou. English is still limited outside business circles, daily life runs on Chinese apps, air quality can dip, and long-stay visas remain difficult. It costs more than Chengdu or Xian.
guangzhou.whoFor: Guangzhou suits the food-obsessed, city-loving nomad who wants a fully-equipped southern Chinese megacity with world-class Cantonese cuisine and excellent regional connectivity. It is ideal if you thrive on dense urban energy, prize dim sum and street food above scenery, and want a base with a major international airport and fast rail to Shenzhen and Hong Kong for Pearl River Delta hopping. The pockets of English and international trade infrastructure make it a bit smoother for business-minded travelers than inland hubs, while the cost stays below Shenzhen and Shanghai. It fits entrepreneurs, importers, and those drawn to commerce and cuisine over postcard sights. It is a poor fit for anyone sensitive to heat and humidity, those wanting a scenic or laid-back setting, or people needing seamless Western connectivity and an easy long-stay visa. Come to Guangzhou for the food, the connectivity, and the megacity buzz; brace for the climate and bring a VPN.

kunming.costOfLiving: Kunming remains one of China's most affordable provincial capitals, and a solo remote worker lives comfortably on roughly $1,000 per month (editorial estimates in USD). A one-bedroom apartment in the city center runs about $300 to $420, while the same outside the core drops to $180 to $280. Groceries at local wet markets are cheap, around $150 to $200 monthly, since Yunnan produce is abundant. Eating out is a bargain: a bowl of crossing-the-bridge rice noodles costs $2 to $4, and a full restaurant meal rarely tops $8. The metro and buses cost under $0.60 a ride, so monthly transport stays near $25. A coworking desk or a membership at a cafe-style space runs $80 to $130. Budget a little extra for a reliable VPN subscription, which is essentially mandatory for accessing Western services.
kunming.whereToWork: Kunming has a smaller coworking scene than Shanghai or Chengdu, but serviced offices and cafe-style shared spaces exist around the university district and Dianchi area. Home wifi and mobile data are fast and cheap, though the crucial caveat is China's firewall: Google, Gmail, WhatsApp, Instagram, and most Western sites are blocked, so a working VPN is non-negotiable. Set one up before you arrive, since VPN provider sites are themselves hard to reach inside the country. A China Mobile or China Unicom SIM gives you strong 4G and 5G almost everywhere for a few dollars. Cafe-work culture is growing, with plenty of independent coffee shops in the Wenlin Street and Green Lake neighborhoods that welcome laptop users. Bring a backup connection plan, and expect occasional VPN slowdowns during sensitive dates when censorship tightens across the country.
kunming.gettingAround: Kunming is flat, walkable in its central districts, and has an expanding metro network that reaches the airport and major neighborhoods for well under a dollar per trip. Buses are extensive and cheap, and the city is far less congested than China's mega-cities. Didi is the dominant ride-hailing app and works smoothly once linked to a local payment method like Alipay or WeChat Pay, with short trips costing $2 to $5. You do not need a car, and driving is impractical for most foreigners anyway. Kunming Changshui International Airport is a major regional hub with direct flights across China and into Southeast Asia, making it a convenient base for wider travel. Shared bikes are everywhere for last-mile hops. Set up mobile payments early, as cash is increasingly awkward and many services assume you are paying by phone.
kunming.visas: China significantly expanded its unilateral visa-free entry in 2024 and 2025, allowing passport holders from many European, Asian, and other countries to enter for up to 30 days without a visa. There is also a generous transit visa-free policy for travelers passing through on the way to a third country. China does not offer any digital nomad visa, and formally working while on a tourist or visa-free entry is not permitted, so treat remote work as a grey area and keep a low profile. Rules here change frequently and depend heavily on your nationality, so verify the current list of eligible countries and exact day limits with an official Chinese embassy or consulate before booking. For longer stays you would need a proper work, business, or study visa arranged in advance. Always confirm the latest policy directly, since these entry rules shift often.
kunming.bestTime: Kunming earns its nickname, the City of Eternal Spring, thanks to a mild subtropical highland climate that stays pleasant almost year-round. Sitting at roughly 1,900 meters elevation, it avoids the brutal summer heat of most Chinese cities and the harsh winters of the north. Daytime temperatures typically hover between 15C and 25C for much of the year. The most comfortable stretch is the dry season from roughly March through May and again from September into November, when skies are clear and flowers bloom. The rainy season runs from June to August, bringing frequent afternoon showers, though rarely the oppressive humidity found elsewhere. Winters are cool and dry, occasionally chilly at night since many buildings lack central heating, so pack a warm layer. Overall there is no truly bad time to visit, but spring and autumn deliver the finest weather for extended stays.
kunming.prosCons: On the plus side, Kunming offers genuinely mild weather year-round, low living costs, clean air relative to many Chinese cities, excellent street food, and easy access to Yunnan's stunning landscapes like Dali, Lijiang, and the rice terraces. The pace is relaxed and the setting green. On the downside, the internet firewall is a constant friction, requiring a reliable VPN just to do normal remote work, and speeds can be inconsistent. English is not widely spoken, so daily life is much smoother with some Mandarin and translation apps. The coworking and international community is smaller than in bigger hubs, so networking takes effort. Bureaucracy around long-term stays is real, and mobile-payment-only norms can trip up newcomers. There is no nomad visa pathway, which limits how long you can legitimately base yourself here without a proper work arrangement.
kunming.whoFor: Kunming suits the adventurous, self-sufficient nomad who values mild weather, low costs, and authentic Chinese life over a ready-made expat bubble. It is ideal if you already speak some Mandarin or are keen to learn, since English support is limited and daily tasks reward language effort. Travelers who want a launchpad for exploring Yunnan's mountains, ethnic-minority towns, and Southeast Asian border regions will love the location. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs uncensored, frictionless internet for their work, since the firewall never fully disappears even with a VPN. It also suits shorter stays given the lack of a nomad visa, making it better as a month-long base than a permanent home. Come here if you prize calm, nature, and cultural immersion, and if you are comfortable navigating a place that runs almost entirely on Chinese-language apps.

curitiba.costOfLiving: Curitiba is one of southern Brazil's more polished cities, and a solo remote worker can live well on about $1,400 per month (editorial estimates in USD). A one-bedroom apartment in central, desirable neighborhoods like Batel or Centro runs roughly $350 to $550, while comparable places further out drop to $250 to $380. Groceries are reasonable at around $200 to $280 monthly, helped by strong local markets and Brazil's cheap produce. Eating out is good value: a hearty prato feito lunch costs $4 to $7, and a per-kilo buffet, a Brazilian staple, runs $6 to $10. Curitiba's celebrated bus system keeps transport cheap, around $30 to $45 a month. A coworking membership typically lands between $90 and $160. Add utilities, mobile data, and some leisure, and the total sits comfortably near the $1,400 mark, less if you cook often and skip the priciest neighborhoods.
curitiba.whereToWork: Curitiba has a mature coworking scene, with numerous shared offices clustered around Batel and the city center offering hot desks, private rooms, and events. As a wealthier, well-organized southern city, its internet infrastructure is strong: fiber home connections are widely available and reliable, and cafe wifi is generally solid. Brazil's mobile networks in cities are good, so a local prepaid SIM from Vivo, Claro, or TIM gives you dependable 4G and growing 5G coverage as a backup. Cafe-work culture is comfortable here, with a thriving specialty-coffee scene, fitting given Curitiba's cool climate makes lingering over a laptop pleasant. Many cafes in Batel and Alto da XV welcome remote workers for a few hours. For serious focus and networking, a coworking membership is worthwhile and connects you to the local startup community. Overall connectivity is among the more reliable you will find in Brazil.
curitiba.gettingAround: Curitiba is famous worldwide for pioneering the Bus Rapid Transit model, and its integrated bus network with tube-shaped stations remains efficient, extensive, and cheap at roughly $1 per ride. The city is also notably walkable in central districts and greener than most, with pedestrian streets and abundant parks. Ride-hailing via Uber and 99 is widespread, affordable, and the easiest way to move at night, with typical trips costing $3 to $7. You do not need a car to live here, and many nomads skip one entirely, relying on buses, walking, and apps. Afonso Pena International Airport, in neighboring Sao Jose dos Pinhais, handles domestic flights and some regional international routes, connecting easily through Sao Paulo hubs. Traffic is lighter than in Rio or Sao Paulo. Between the reliable transit and cheap ride-hailing, getting around is one of Curitiba's genuine strengths.
curitiba.visas: Brazil offers a Digital Nomad Visa valid for one year and renewable for another, aimed at remote workers employed by companies outside Brazil. The main requirement is proof of income of roughly $1,500 per month or savings of around $18,000, plus health insurance, applied for through a Brazilian consulate or, in some cases, on arrival. For shorter stays, many nationalities including most Europeans get 90 days visa-free as tourists, often extendable by another 90 days per year. Note that some passport holders, and recently citizens of the US, Canada, and Australia, may face reintroduced visa requirements, so this is exactly the kind of rule that shifts. Always confirm the latest income thresholds, document list, and your own nationality's requirements with an official Brazilian consulate before making plans. The nomad visa is the cleanest legal route for basing yourself in Curitiba beyond the tourist window.
curitiba.bestTime: Curitiba sits on a high plateau in Brazil's south and has a noticeably cooler, more temperate climate than the tropical northeast or Rio. Expect four distinct seasons and frequent temperature swings within a single day, so layers are your friend year-round. Summer, from December to March, is mild and pleasant by Brazilian standards, with warm days rarely oppressive but fairly frequent rain. Winter, from June to August, is genuinely cool, with nights sometimes dropping near freezing and damp, grey stretches, so it is the season most people find least comfortable. The most agreeable months are the shoulder seasons of spring, September to November, and autumn, April to May, when the weather is mild, drier, and the city's many parks look their best. If you dislike cold and damp, avoid deep winter. Otherwise Curitiba is a comfortable, sweat-free base almost any month.
curitiba.prosCons: Curitiba's strengths are real: it is clean, safe by Brazilian standards, exceptionally green with world-class parks, well organized, and has excellent public transit and reliable internet. The cool climate is a relief if you dislike tropical heat, and the coffee and food scenes are strong. The city feels calm and orderly. On the downside, that same cool, grey winter weather disappoints anyone expecting beaches and constant sun, and Curitiba has no coastline. The nomad and expat community is smaller than in Florianopolis, Rio, or Sao Paulo, so social life takes more initiative. Portuguese is essential, since English is not widely spoken. Some visitors find the city a touch quiet or lacking the vibrant energy of Brazil's more famous destinations. If you crave nightlife, warmth, and a big international crowd, Curitiba may feel understated compared with its flashier Brazilian rivals.
curitiba.whoFor: Curitiba suits the nomad who prioritizes livability over spectacle: someone who wants a safe, clean, well-run city with reliable internet, great parks, and a temperate climate rather than beaches and heat. It is ideal for focused remote workers, digital professionals, and anyone who finds tropical humidity draining and appreciates cool evenings and four real seasons. Coffee lovers and park-and-cycle types will feel at home. It rewards those willing to learn some Portuguese and build their own social circle, since the international community is modest. It is a weaker choice for beach seekers, party-focused travelers, or anyone wanting a large ready-made nomad scene, who would be happier in Florianopolis or Rio. Choose Curitiba if you value calm, order, green space, and a comfortable base for exploring southern Brazil, and if a mild, sometimes chilly climate sounds like a feature rather than a drawback.

fortaleza.costOfLiving: Fortaleza, a large coastal city in Brazil's northeast, offers beach living at a lower cost than the south, and a solo remote worker manages well on around $1,300 per month (editorial estimates in USD). A one-bedroom apartment near the beach in Meireles or Aldeota runs roughly $300 to $500, while further from the coast you find places for $200 to $320. Groceries cost about $180 to $260 monthly, with cheap tropical fruit, fish, and produce widely available. Eating out is inexpensive: a set lunch runs $4 to $7, and fresh seafood or a beachside meal stays affordable. Local buses cost around $1, keeping monthly transport near $30 to $50 if you mix in ride-hailing. Coworking memberships run $80 to $150. Air conditioning and its electricity bill are a real line item here given the year-round heat, so budget a bit extra for cooling and utilities.
fortaleza.whereToWork: Fortaleza has a growing coworking scene concentrated in the Meireles, Aldeota, and Praia de Iracema areas near the beach, offering desks, meeting rooms, and a local startup community. As a major Brazilian city, its internet is generally good, with fiber home connections common and reliable, though quality can vary more by building than in the wealthier south. A prepaid SIM from Vivo, Claro, or TIM provides solid urban 4G and 5G as a dependable backup. Cafe-work culture exists along the beachfront and in Aldeota, with air-conditioned cafes being especially welcome given the heat. Many nomads value a coworking space here not just for the wifi but for the reliable air conditioning during long working days. Connectivity in central and beachfront neighborhoods is dependable enough for video calls, though it is wise to test your specific apartment's connection before committing to a longer lease.
fortaleza.gettingAround: Fortaleza is a sprawling city, and while the beachfront districts of Meireles and Iracema are pleasantly walkable with a long seaside promenade, getting across town requires transport. There is a limited metro and an extensive bus network, with fares around $1, though buses can be crowded and slow. Most nomads lean on ride-hailing, with Uber and 99 both cheap and widely available; typical trips cost $3 to $8. You do not strictly need a car if you base yourself near the beach and use apps, though a car helps for exploring the famous dune beaches and coastline beyond the city. Pinto Martins International Airport connects Fortaleza to the rest of Brazil and increasingly to Europe, making it a convenient Atlantic gateway. For day trips to spots like Cumbuco or Jericoacoara, arrange a transfer or rental, since public options thin out fast.
fortaleza.visas: Brazil's Digital Nomad Visa applies here just as anywhere in the country: it grants a one-year, renewable stay for remote workers employed by foreign companies, requiring proof of income around $1,500 per month or equivalent savings, plus valid health insurance. You apply through a Brazilian consulate abroad, and it is the cleanest legal route for a longer Fortaleza stay. For shorter visits, many nationalities including most Europeans enter visa-free as tourists for 90 days, frequently extendable to 180 days within a year. However, visa requirements for some countries, including recently the US, Canada, and Australia, have been in flux, so do not assume. Because these thresholds and reciprocity rules change, always verify the current income requirement, document checklist, and your own passport's status directly with an official Brazilian consulate or the immigration authority before you travel or commit to a rental.
fortaleza.bestTime: Fortaleza sits close to the equator and is hot and sunny essentially year-round, with temperatures typically in the high 20s to low 30s Celsius every month, tempered by a near-constant sea breeze. Unlike southern Brazil, there is no cool season, so if you dislike heat, be prepared for it all the time. The year splits into a wet season and a dry season rather than hot and cold. The rainy months run roughly from February through May, when heavy showers are common, though they often pass quickly. The best time to visit is the dry season from around July to December, when you get reliable sunshine, lower humidity, and ideal beach and dune conditions. September through November are especially good. Wind sports enthusiasts favor the windy second half of the year. Whenever you come, plan for strong sun and pack accordingly.
fortaleza.prosCons: Fortaleza's appeal is straightforward: warm weather every single day, long urban beaches, a lively seaside promenade, fresh seafood, low costs, and easy access to spectacular dune-lined coastline like Jericoacoara. The constant sea breeze takes the edge off the heat, and flights to Europe are handy. On the downside, the relentless heat and, in season, heavy rains can wear on some people, and there is no escape into cool weather. Safety is a genuine consideration, as Fortaleza has higher crime rates than the calmer southern cities, so you must be street-smart about neighborhoods and nighttime movement. The city sprawls, English is limited, and the nomad community is smaller and less established than in Florianopolis or Rio. Air conditioning is close to a necessity, adding to costs. It is a trade-off of beach lifestyle and value against heat, sprawl, and safety caution.
fortaleza.whoFor: Fortaleza suits the sun-loving, beach-focused nomad who wants warm weather guaranteed year-round, affordable coastal living, and a base for exploring northeastern Brazil's stunning dunes and lagoons. It is a natural fit for kitesurfers and windsurfers, who flock to the region for its steady winds, and for anyone happy trading cooler climates for permanent summer. Budget-conscious remote workers get real value here compared with southern or international beach hubs. It rewards those who speak some Portuguese and are comfortable staying alert about safety in a big northeastern city. It is a weaker choice for anyone sensitive to heat, wanting a large polished expat scene, or prioritizing safety and walkable compactness above all, who might prefer Florianopolis. Come to Fortaleza if endless sun, beaches, seafood, and low costs outweigh the heat, sprawl, and need for everyday street awareness.

belohorizonte.costOfLiving: Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, is a large inland city offering strong value, and a solo remote worker lives comfortably on about $1,300 per month (editorial estimates in USD). A one-bedroom apartment in sought-after central areas like Savassi or Funcionarios runs roughly $300 to $480, while neighborhoods further out drop to $200 to $320. Groceries cost around $180 to $260 monthly, with the region's famous produce and markets keeping quality high and prices low. Eating out is a highlight and a bargain: a generous prato feito or per-kilo lunch runs $5 to $9, and the city's legendary bar food, or comida de boteco, is cheap and plentiful. Buses and the limited metro keep transport near $30 to $50 monthly, supplemented by ride-hailing. Coworking memberships run $80 to $150. Minas food culture means eating out often is both a pleasure and easy on the budget here.
belohorizonte.whereToWork: Belo Horizonte has a solid coworking ecosystem, much of it clustered in and around Savassi, the city's hip commercial and nightlife hub, alongside spaces in the central business districts. As one of Brazil's largest metros, its internet is generally reliable, with fiber home connections widely available and cafe wifi usually dependable in the better neighborhoods. A prepaid SIM from Vivo, Claro, or TIM delivers good urban 4G and 5G coverage as a solid backup for calls. Cafe-work culture thrives, helped by Minas Gerais's serious coffee heritage and a dense scene of bakeries and cafes where lingering with a laptop is normal. Savassi in particular has plenty of laptop-friendly spots that transition from daytime workspace to evening bar. For longer focus sessions and meeting local founders, a coworking membership is worthwhile, plugging you into the city's genuine startup and tech community, one of the more active in Brazil.
belohorizonte.gettingAround: Belo Horizonte is a big, hilly city, and while central neighborhoods like Savassi and Funcionarios are walkable and lively, the terrain and sprawl mean you will use transport for longer trips. There is a single metro line of limited reach plus an extensive bus network with fares around $1, though buses can be slow and crowded. Ride-hailing through Uber and 99 is the go-to for most nomads, being cheap, quick, and safe for night moves, with typical trips costing $3 to $8. You do not need a car to live centrally, though one helps for weekend trips into the beautiful Minas countryside and historic towns like Ouro Preto. Tancredo Neves International Airport, at Confins about 40 minutes out, connects the city domestically and with some international routes. Between walkable central districts and cheap ride-hailing, daily mobility is manageable without owning a vehicle.
belohorizonte.visas: As with anywhere in Brazil, Belo Horizonte falls under the country's national Digital Nomad Visa, which allows remote workers employed by foreign companies to stay for one year, renewable for a second. You will need to show income of roughly $1,500 per month or sufficient savings, plus health insurance, and apply through a Brazilian consulate abroad. This is the most straightforward legal path for a longer stay. For shorter visits, many nationalities including most Europeans enter visa-free for 90 days as tourists, often extendable to 180 days within a twelve-month period. Be aware that visa reciprocity rules have recently shifted for some countries, including the US, Canada, and Australia, so your situation depends on your passport. Because income thresholds and entry rules change, always verify the current requirements and document list directly with an official Brazilian consulate or immigration authority before booking or signing a lease.
belohorizonte.bestTime: Belo Horizonte enjoys a pleasant highland tropical climate, sitting at around 850 meters elevation, which keeps temperatures milder and more comfortable than Brazil's steamy coastal cities. The year divides into a wet season and a dry season rather than hot and cold extremes. The rainy season runs from roughly October to March, bringing warm days and frequent, sometimes heavy afternoon showers along with higher humidity. The dry season, from about April to September, is the sweet spot: warm, sunny days, low humidity, cooler and very pleasant evenings, and little rain. Those dry-season months are the best time to base yourself here, with June and July occasionally cool at night, so pack a light jacket. Summers are warm but rarely oppressive thanks to the altitude. If you want to avoid the wettest, most humid stretch, steer clear of the peak of the rainy season around December and January.
belohorizonte.prosCons: Belo Horizonte's strengths are its famous food and bar culture, genuinely warm and welcoming locals, a pleasant highland climate, strong value for money, a real tech and startup scene, and easy access to the stunning colonial towns and mountains of Minas Gerais. It feels authentically Brazilian rather than touristy. On the downside, it is a large, sprawling, hilly city with limited metro coverage, so you depend on buses and ride-hailing. There is no beach and fewer marquee sights than Rio, so its appeal is more about lifestyle and food than postcard attractions. The nomad and international community is smaller than in coastal hotspots, and English is not widely spoken, making Portuguese important. As in any big Brazilian city, you should stay aware of safety in certain areas and at night. It rewards those who value substance, cuisine, and local life over obvious tourist glamour.
belohorizonte.whoFor: Belo Horizonte suits the nomad who wants an authentic, food-obsessed Brazilian city over a beach-resort or heavily touristed scene. It is perfect for anyone who loves eating and drinking out, since the boteco bar culture and Minas cuisine are among the best in the country and remarkably affordable. It fits sociable travelers happy to learn some Portuguese and connect with warm locals and an active startup community rather than lean on a big expat bubble. The mild highland climate appeals to those who find coastal heat and humidity tiring. It is a launchpad for exploring historic colonial towns and mountain scenery. It is a weaker pick for beach lovers, first-time visitors wanting famous landmarks, or anyone needing a large ready-made international nomad crowd. Choose Belo Horizonte if great food, genuine local culture, good value, and a comfortable climate matter more to you than beaches and tourist fame.

kolkata.costOfLiving: Kolkata is one of India's most affordable major cities, and a solo remote worker can live well on around $700 per month (editorial estimates in USD). A one-bedroom apartment in a central area like Park Street, Ballygunge, or Salt Lake runs roughly $150 to $280, while outside the core you find places for $90 to $160. Groceries are very cheap at around $80 to $130 monthly, helped by abundant local markets. Eating out is where Kolkata shines: legendary street food like kathi rolls and puchka costs under $1, and a full restaurant meal rarely exceeds $5 to $8. Public transport, including the metro, buses, and iconic trams, costs mere cents per ride, keeping monthly transit under $25 even with regular ride-hailing. Coworking desks run a modest $60 to $110 monthly. The low rent and dirt-cheap, extraordinary food make Kolkata one of the best-value nomad bases anywhere in Asia.
kolkata.whereToWork: Kolkata has a developing coworking scene, with spaces concentrated around Salt Lake Sector V, the city's IT hub, plus options near Park Street and the central business district offering desks and meeting rooms. The important caveat is that internet reliability in India is variable: a good fiber connection at home or in a coworking space is fine, but power cuts and inconsistent building wiring happen, so carry a backup. A prepaid 4G SIM from Jio or Airtel is cheap, delivers strong data across the city, and is essential insurance for keeping video calls alive when the wifi falters. Buy one on arrival with your passport. Cafe-work culture exists in the more modern coffee chains and Park Street cafes, though it is less entrenched than in Bengaluru. For dependable connectivity and air conditioning during the intense heat, a coworking membership is the safest bet for serious remote work here.
kolkata.gettingAround: Kolkata has India's oldest metro, now expanding, which is cheap, fast, and a lifesaver for crossing the congested city, with fares of just a few cents. The city also runs an extensive bus network and the historic tram, a charming if slow relic. Central areas around Park Street are walkable, though pavements are crowded and traffic is chaotic, so walking is more sightseeing than efficient transport. Ride-hailing via Uber and Ola is cheap and widely used, alongside the ubiquitous yellow Ambassador taxis and auto-rickshaws for short hops; app trips often cost just $1 to $4. You absolutely do not need a car, and driving yourself here would be stressful and unnecessary. Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport connects Kolkata across India and to regional international destinations. Between the metro, cheap ride-hailing, and rickshaws, getting around is inexpensive, if best approached with patience for the traffic.
kolkata.visas: India makes short stays easy through its e-Tourist Visa, applied for entirely online in advance, with options ranging from 30 days up to multi-year multiple-entry validity depending on your nationality. It is quick, affordable, and the standard route for most visitors. Crucially, India has no dedicated digital nomad visa, and working remotely while on a tourist visa sits in a legal grey area: the tourist visa is officially for tourism and recreation, not employment, even if your employer and income are entirely outside India. Many nomads do work quietly on tourist visas, but understand it is not formally sanctioned, so keep a low profile and do not seek local income. For anything longer term or for actual India-based work, you would need an appropriate business or employment visa. Because visa categories and e-Visa eligibility change, always verify the current rules and your nationality's options on the official Indian government e-Visa portal before applying.
kolkata.bestTime: Kolkata has a tropical climate with a punishing hot and humid season, so timing your stay matters more here than in many cities. The clearly best months are the cool, dry winter from November to February, when daytime temperatures are pleasant, humidity drops, and the city is at its most livable and festive. This is the ideal window for a longer base. Avoid the pre-monsoon stretch from March to May, when heat and humidity become oppressive, with temperatures pushing into the high 30s Celsius and sticky, draining conditions. The monsoon, from June to September, brings heavy rain, flooding in parts of the low-lying city, and relentless humidity, making it the least comfortable and most disruptive time. October offers a pleasant, celebratory shoulder period around Durga Puja. In short, come in winter for comfort, and steer well clear of the hot, humid monsoon months if you can.
kolkata.prosCons: Kolkata's strengths are its remarkable affordability, extraordinary street food, deep cultural and intellectual heritage, grand colonial architecture, and warm, famously welcoming, literary-minded locals. It offers an authentic, un-sanitized Indian experience at rock-bottom prices, with a metro and cheap transport that make it navigable. On the downside, the summer heat and monsoon humidity are genuinely brutal, air pollution and congestion are real issues, and the infrastructure feels older and more worn than in Bengaluru or Delhi. Internet and power can be inconsistent, so backups are essential. The nomad and international community is small and the coworking scene modest, so you will not find a big ready-made expat crowd. The pace, noise, and crowds can overwhelm newcomers to India.
