It is a city that rewards curiosity and patience, trading polish and convenience for culture, character, and value that are hard to match anywhere else.
kolkata.whoFor: Kolkata suits the culturally curious, budget-minded nomad who wants an immersive, authentic Indian experience rather than a comfortable, ready-made expat hub. It is ideal for lovers of food, history, literature, art, and street life, since the city rewards wandering, conversation, and exploration at every turn. Extreme value seekers will stretch their money remarkably far here. It works best for experienced travelers, ideally with some prior India exposure, who can handle heat, crowds, noise, and variable infrastructure with patience and good humor. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting slick modern amenities, guaranteed fast internet, a large nomad social scene, or an easy first introduction to India, who would be better served by Bengaluru or Goa. Come to Kolkata if you value soul, culture, incredible cheap food, and genuine human warmth over convenience, and if you visit during the cooler, comfortable winter months.

chennai.costOfLiving: Chennai runs around $750 per month for a comfortable single nomad. A furnished one-bedroom in a central area like Nungambakkam or T. Nagar costs roughly $250 to $400, with cheaper options further out. Eating local is very affordable, and a filling South Indian meal can run $2 to $4, so budget $180 to $250 for food if you mix home cooking, cafes, and the odd restaurant. A prepaid SIM with generous data is about $3 to $5 monthly. Add $40 to $70 for a coworking hot desk, plus transport, utilities, and air conditioning during the hot months. Air conditioning pushes electricity bills up noticeably from March through June. Domestic help and laundry are cheap. You can live on less by choosing a shared flat and eating at local messes, or spend more for a sea-facing apartment and frequent cabs.
chennai.whereToWork: Chennai has a solid coworking scene concentrated around Guindy, Nungambakkam, and the OMR tech corridor, with day passes and monthly hot desks widely available. Home wifi is generally decent in the city but can be inconsistent during monsoon and outages, so keep a backup 4G or 5G SIM topped up with data as a reliable fallback. Mobile coverage is strong and cheap, which matters when fixed lines wobble. Cafe culture leans toward filter coffee spots and modern cafes in Besant Nagar and Alwarpet where you can plug in for a few hours, though not every place welcomes long laptop sessions. Power cuts still happen occasionally, so a coworking space with backup power is the safest bet for calls. Working from your apartment is fine most days, but treat unmetered fixed broadband as a bonus rather than a guarantee.
chennai.gettingAround: Chennai is spread out and fairly flat, but heat and traffic make walking long distances tiring outside cooler months. The metro is clean, cheap, and expanding, though it does not yet cover every neighborhood, so many nomads rely on ride-hailing. Ola and Uber both operate widely, and autorickshaws are everywhere, though metered fares are inconsistent, so agree a price or use the app. Suburban trains and city buses are extremely cheap but crowded and less intuitive for newcomers. Chennai International Airport is well connected domestically and to Southeast Asia and the Gulf, roughly 30 to 45 minutes from the center depending on traffic, and reachable by metro. Owning or renting a two-wheeler is common among longer-stay residents but traffic is chaotic. For most short-term nomads, a mix of metro plus app cabs and autos covers daily life comfortably.
chennai.visas: India has no dedicated digital nomad visa. Most visitors enter on the e-Tourist Visa, applied for online before travel, available in 30-day, one-year, and five-year variants depending on nationality. It is straightforward to obtain and is the standard route for nomads staying a few weeks to months. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a tourist visa sits in a legal grey area that Indian rules do not clearly address, so understand you are not formally authorized to work and weigh that risk yourself. For any local employment or paid activity inside India you would need a proper employment or business visa. Rules, permitted stay lengths, and registration requirements change, and some longer stays trigger FRRO registration, so always verify the current requirements on the official Indian government visa portal before booking and again close to travel.
chennai.bestTime: The most comfortable window in Chennai is November through February, when temperatures ease and humidity drops to bearable levels, making this the clear peak for visitors. March through June is hot and very humid, with pre-monsoon heat that can feel punishing, so avoid this stretch if you are heat-sensitive. Chennai gets most of its rain from the northeast monsoon between October and December, and heavy downpours can cause flooding and disrupt travel, so factor that in if you visit late in the year. Coastal humidity is a constant, meaning even pleasant months feel sticky compared to inland India. If you want festivals, the Margazhi music and dance season peaks in December and January, coinciding with the best weather. For remote work with reliable power and comfortable evenings, aim for the December to February sweet spot and treat everything else as a compromise.
chennai.prosCons: Chennai's strengths are low costs, excellent and cheap South Indian food, a genuine tech industry with real coworking options, warm and orderly local culture, and good air links to Southeast Asia and the Gulf. The beaches and the nearby heritage sites of Mahabalipuram add appeal. On the downside, the heat and humidity are relentless for much of the year, traffic is heavy, and the city is more conservative and less overtly nomad-oriented than places like Goa or Bangalore. English is widely spoken, but Tamil dominates daily life. Wifi can be patchy, power cuts still occur, and monsoon flooding is a real risk. Nightlife is limited compared to other metros. It is a practical, affordable base with authentic culture rather than a polished nomad hub, rewarding travelers who value substance and value over scene and convenience.
chennai.whoFor: Chennai suits budget-conscious nomads who want an authentic South Indian city rather than a curated nomad bubble. It works well for people in tech who value proximity to a real industry, for food lovers drawn to filter coffee and vegetarian and Chettinad cuisine, and for travelers interested in temples, classical arts, and heritage. If you tolerate heat and humidity well and can handle occasional infrastructure hiccups with a backup SIM, you will find great value here. It is a strong pick for longer stays where low costs compound. It is less ideal for those who need a buzzing party scene, cool weather, or a large ready-made international community. Solo travelers and couples who like calm, orderly cities will feel comfortable, and the strong English usage lowers the language barrier for getting set up and finding services quickly.

hyderabad.costOfLiving: Hyderabad sits around $800 per month for a single nomad living comfortably. A furnished one-bedroom in a good area like Gachibowli, Madhapur, or Banjara Hills runs roughly $280 to $450, with more affordable flats a little further from the tech hubs. Food is a highlight and a bargain, and you can eat well on $180 to $260 a month, whether that means famous biryani, local tiffin, or the many mid-range restaurants. A data-heavy SIM is around $3 to $5 monthly. Budget $45 to $75 for a coworking hot desk, plus utilities, air conditioning in summer, and transport. Electricity bills climb during the hot April to June stretch when air conditioning runs constantly. Groceries, domestic help, and laundry are inexpensive. You can trim costs with a shared flat and local eateries, or spend more for a modern apartment near the IT corridor with easy access to malls and cafes.
hyderabad.whereToWork: Hyderabad has one of India's better coworking ecosystems, clustered around HITEC City, Madhapur, and Gachibowli where the IT industry concentrates, so hot desks and day passes are plentiful and professional. Fixed broadband in these tech areas is generally reliable, but service can still drop during outages or storms, so keep a backup 4G or 5G SIM loaded with data as insurance for important calls. Mobile coverage is strong and cheap across the city. Cafe culture is growing, with plenty of modern cafes near the tech corridor and in Jubilee Hills that tolerate laptop work, alongside traditional Irani cafes better suited to a chai break than a long session. Many coworking spaces run backup power, which matters during occasional cuts. For remote workers, basing yourself near HITEC City gives the best combination of connectivity, backup infrastructure, and workspace choice.
hyderabad.gettingAround: Hyderabad is large and car-oriented, and the tech districts sit well outside the historic center, so distances are significant. The metro is modern, clean, and covers key corridors including parts of the IT belt, making it a good backbone for daily travel, though it does not reach everywhere. Ride-hailing through Ola and Uber is widespread and affordable, and autorickshaws fill the gaps, though you should use the app meter or agree fares. Traffic is heavy during peak hours, especially around HITEC City. Rajiv Gandhi International Airport is one of India's better airports, well connected domestically and internationally, but it sits far south of the city, so allow 45 to 75 minutes by cab depending on traffic. Two-wheelers are popular with longer-stay residents. For most nomads, combining the metro with app cabs and the occasional auto covers daily life without needing your own vehicle.
hyderabad.visas: India has no digital nomad visa, so Hyderabad visitors use the e-Tourist Visa, applied for online before arrival in 30-day, one-year, or five-year forms depending on nationality. It is easy to obtain and is the usual route for stays ranging from a few weeks to several months. Working remotely for an overseas employer while holding a tourist visa falls into a legal grey area that Indian regulations do not clearly resolve, so recognize you are not formally permitted to work and decide how comfortable you are with that ambiguity. Local employment or any India-based paid activity requires a proper employment or business visa instead. Permitted stay lengths, entry conditions, and any registration duties can change, and some extended stays require FRRO registration, so confirm the current rules on the official Indian government visa portal before you book and again shortly before you travel.
hyderabad.bestTime: The best time to be in Hyderabad is roughly October through February, when the weather is mild, dry, and pleasant for both work and sightseeing, marking the clear peak season. Hyderabad sits on the Deccan plateau, so it is generally a touch less humid than coastal Chennai, which makes the cool season especially comfortable. Avoid the peak heat of April through June, when temperatures climb high and air conditioning becomes essential all day. The southwest monsoon brings rain mainly from June to September, which cools things down but can cause waterlogging and traffic snarls, so it is a mixed period. Winter nights can feel genuinely cool by Indian standards, a welcome change. For the most productive remote-work stint with comfortable evenings and minimal weather disruption, target November to February, and treat the pre-monsoon summer as the stretch to plan around rather than through.
hyderabad.prosCons: Hyderabad's pluses include a strong and modern tech economy with excellent coworking, relatively good infrastructure in the IT districts, legendary and affordable food, a plateau climate that is milder than the coast, and a clean, expanding metro. The historic Charminar area, forts, and lakes give it real character beyond the office parks. Costs stay low for the quality on offer. Drawbacks include a sprawling layout with long distances between the old city and the tech belt, heavy peak-hour traffic, and summer heat that demands constant air conditioning. It is more of a business and IT city than a leisure nomad hotspot, so the ready-made international scene is smaller than in Goa or Bangalore. English is widely used alongside Telugu and Urdu. Occasional power cuts and monsoon waterlogging remain nuisances. Overall it balances practicality, value, and culture well for a working base.
hyderabad.whoFor: Hyderabad fits nomads who want a well-run, affordable Indian city with a genuine tech backbone and solid coworking rather than a beach-party crowd. It suits remote workers in software who value proximity to a real industry and reliable-enough infrastructure near HITEC City, plus food lovers eager to work through the city's famous biryani and rich culinary mix. History and culture fans get the Charminar, Golconda Fort, and lakeside evenings. The milder plateau climate appeals to those who find coastal humidity draining. It is a good long-stay value base where low costs add up over months. It suits solo travelers and couples comfortable navigating a large, car-oriented city with cabs and the metro. It is less suited to people seeking a compact walkable town, cool mountain weather, or a large established international nomad community, since Hyderabad is more workmanlike than scene-driven.

ahmedabad.costOfLiving: Ahmedabad is among India's better-value cities, running around $650 per month for a comfortable single nomad. A furnished one-bedroom in a decent area such as Navrangpura, Satellite, or near the riverfront costs roughly $200 to $350, with cheaper options further out. Food is very affordable, and Gujarati thalis, street snacks, and local eateries let you eat well on $150 to $220 a month, though note this is a largely vegetarian city so meat and especially alcohol are hard to find. A generous data SIM is about $3 to $5 monthly. Budget $35 to $65 for a coworking hot desk, plus utilities and heavy air conditioning use in the intense summer. Electricity bills spike badly from March through June. Groceries and domestic help are cheap. You can live comfortably on modest spending here, and the low rents make Ahmedabad one of the most economical metro bases in the country.
ahmedabad.whereToWork: Ahmedabad has a growing but smaller coworking scene than the big tech metros, with spaces concentrated around Navrangpura, C.G. Road, Prahlad Nagar, and the SG Highway corridor offering hot desks and day passes. Fixed broadband in the city is reasonable, but reliability can dip during outages and the hot season, so keep a backup 4G or 5G SIM loaded with data for critical calls, which is wise across India. Mobile coverage is strong and cheap. Cafe culture is developing, with modern cafes along C.G. Road and in newer commercial areas where laptop work is tolerated, though the city is more business-driven than cafe-lounging in character. Being a dry state, do not expect cafe-bar hybrids for evening work sessions. Coworking spaces with backup power are the safest choice during occasional cuts. Basing near Prahlad Nagar or SG Highway gives good access to workspaces and amenities.
ahmedabad.gettingAround: Ahmedabad is relatively flat and has invested in transport, including a growing metro and the BRTS bus rapid transit system that runs on dedicated lanes and is cheap and reasonably efficient. Still, the city is spread out and summer heat makes long walks unpleasant much of the year. Ride-hailing via Ola and Uber works well and is affordable, and autorickshaws are plentiful, though you should use app meters or agree fares in advance. The metro is clean and expanding but does not yet reach every area. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport sits close to the city, typically 20 to 40 minutes from central areas, with good domestic links and some international routes to the Gulf. Two-wheelers are common among residents. For most nomads, a combination of app cabs, autos, and the BRTS or metro covers daily needs comfortably without owning a vehicle.
ahmedabad.visas: India offers no digital nomad visa, so visitors to Ahmedabad rely on the e-Tourist Visa, applied for online ahead of travel in 30-day, one-year, or five-year versions depending on nationality. It is simple to obtain and is the standard path for stays from a few weeks to several months. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a tourist visa occupies a legal grey area that Indian rules do not clearly address, so understand you are not formally authorized to work and judge that risk for yourself. Any local employment or India-based paid work requires a proper employment or business visa instead. Allowed stay durations, entry rules, and possible registration steps can change over time, and certain longer stays require FRRO registration, so always check the current requirements on the official Indian government visa portal before booking and again just before you travel.
ahmedabad.bestTime: The comfortable season in Ahmedabad is November through February, when the weather turns mild and dry, making it the clear best window for visiting and working. Gujarat is a hot, dry state, and the pre-monsoon stretch from March through June is genuinely punishing, with high temperatures that make air conditioning essential and outdoor activity difficult, so avoid this period if you can. The southwest monsoon arrives around late June and runs through September, bringing relief and some rain, though the city stays drier than coastal India. Winter is the highlight for events too, with the famous Uttarayan kite festival in January and Navratri in autumn drawing crowds. The dry heat is intense but at least less sticky than coastal humidity. For a productive remote-work stay with tolerable evenings and cultural festivals, aim squarely at the November to February window and plan around the brutal summer.
ahmedabad.prosCons: Ahmedabad's strengths are very low costs, some of India's best vegetarian food, strong and improving public transport with the BRTS and metro, a nearby and convenient airport, and a rich heritage as a UNESCO-recognized historic city with the Sabarmati riverfront and Gandhi's ashram. It is safe, orderly, and business-friendly. The main drawbacks are extreme dry-season heat, a smaller coworking and international nomad scene than the tech metros, and the practical realities of a dry, largely vegetarian state, meaning no easy access to alcohol and limited meat options, which some travelers find restrictive. Nightlife is minimal by design. English is widely used in business alongside Gujarati and Hindi. The city is more industrious than glamorous, appealing to those who value substance and value over scene. Overall it rewards budget-focused, culturally curious nomads who do not need a party lifestyle.
ahmedabad.whoFor: Ahmedabad suits budget-minded nomads who want an affordable, safe, and authentic Indian city with strong food and deep heritage rather than a nomad party hub. It is a natural fit for vegetarians, who will find some of the best plant-based food in the country, and for travelers happy in a dry state where alcohol is not part of the routine. It works for people drawn to history, textiles, architecture, and festivals like Uttarayan and Navratri, and for those who appreciate genuinely good public transport in an Indian metro. The very low rents make it excellent for cost-focused long stays. It is less ideal for anyone who needs nightlife, a large established international community, meat-heavy dining, or cool weather, since summers are severe. Solo travelers and couples who value calm, order, and value over buzz will feel at home here quickly.

tashkent.costOfLiving: Tashkent runs around $900 per month for a comfortable single nomad, higher than Indian metros but still good value for a capital. A furnished one-bedroom in a central district costs roughly $350 to $600, with Soviet-era apartments cheaper and modern builds pricier. Food is affordable, and hearty local meals of plov, shashlik, and fresh bread and produce let you eat well on $200 to $300 a month, especially if you shop the bustling bazaars like Chorsu. A local SIM with generous data is inexpensive, around $5 to $10 monthly. Budget $60 to $120 for a coworking hot desk where available, plus utilities, which climb in the cold winter for heating. The metro and taxis are cheap. English is limited, so learning some Russian or Uzbek helps with markets and services. Overall, Tashkent offers solid value with a comfortable, spacious feel and low daily costs outside rent.
tashkent.whereToWork: Tashkent's coworking scene is small but emerging, with a handful of spaces in central business districts offering hot desks, though options are far fewer than in established nomad hubs, so research availability before arriving. Home internet has improved substantially and fixed broadband in the capital is generally workable, but speeds and reliability still lag behind top nomad destinations, so keep a data-loaded mobile SIM as a backup for calls. Mobile coverage in the city is decent and cheap. Cafe culture is growing, with modern coffee shops in central areas where you can work for a few hours, alongside traditional teahouses better suited to relaxing than long laptop sessions. English is limited among staff, so a translation app smooths ordering and asking about wifi. For reliable video calls, a central apartment with a tested connection plus a backup SIM is the pragmatic setup, since dedicated coworking coverage is thinner than you may be used to.
tashkent.gettingAround: Tashkent is a spacious, orderly capital with wide boulevards and one of the region's highlights, an inexpensive and famously ornate metro system that is clean, safe, and easy to use once you learn the lines. Buses and marshrutka minibuses fill the gaps cheaply. The city is fairly walkable in central districts, though it is spread out overall. Yandex Go is the dominant ride-hailing app and is cheap and reliable, making taxis an easy default, while informal street taxis also operate but require haggling and some Russian. Tashkent International Airport sits close to the center, usually 20 to 40 minutes away, with growing connections across Central Asia, Russia, the Gulf, and some European and Asian cities. High-speed trains link Tashkent to Samarkand and Bukhara, making domestic travel comfortable. For daily life, the metro plus Yandex Go covers almost everything affordably and without stress.
tashkent.visas: Uzbekistan has made entry easy for many travelers, offering 30-day visa-free stays for a long list of nationalities, which covers most short to medium nomad trips without paperwork. Those not eligible for visa-free entry can typically apply for an e-visa online in advance, which is straightforward. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa, so remote work is done on tourist entry, and as with most countries that means you are not formally authorized to work locally, so weigh that as you would elsewhere. For stays beyond the visa-free or e-visa window you would need to look into extensions or other permit categories, which are more involved. Registration requirements historically applied to visitors, often handled automatically by hotels, so if you rent privately confirm whether you must register your stay. Visa-free lists, durations, and registration rules change, so verify the current terms on official Uzbek government sources before you travel.
tashkent.bestTime: Tashkent has a continental climate with hot summers and cold winters, so the shoulder seasons of spring and autumn are clearly the best times to visit. Spring, roughly April into early June, brings mild temperatures, green landscapes, and blooming surroundings, making it ideal for both work and exploring the wider country. Autumn, around September into November, is similarly pleasant, with comfortable temperatures and the bonus of fresh harvest produce and fruit filling the bazaars. Summers from June through August get hot and dry, with temperatures that can climb high and make midday activity draining, though evenings cool off. Winters from December through February are genuinely cold, with freezing temperatures and some snow, so heating costs rise and outdoor time shrinks. For the most comfortable stay and easy day trips to Samarkand and Bukhara, target the April to June or September to November windows and avoid the extremes of deep summer and winter.
tashkent.prosCons: Tashkent's appeal lies in strong value, a spacious and safe capital, a superb and cheap metro, excellent and affordable food, warm local hospitality, and easy rail access to the Silk Road cities of Samarkand and Bukhara. Visa-free entry for many nationalities lowers the friction of arriving. Costs outside rent are low and the pace is relaxed. On the downside, the coworking and international nomad scene is small and still developing, English is limited so you will lean on Russian, Uzbek, or translation apps, and internet reliability, while improved, still trails top destinations. Winters are cold and summers are hot, narrowing the ideal window. Some bureaucratic quirks like stay registration linger. It is an off-the-beaten-path base rather than a polished hub, rewarding independent travelers who value authenticity, culture, and value over a ready-made community and seamless infrastructure.
tashkent.whoFor: Tashkent suits adventurous, independent nomads drawn to Central Asia and the Silk Road who want an affordable, safe, and culturally rich base rather than a well-worn nomad circuit stop. It fits people comfortable navigating limited English with some Russian or a translation app, and travelers who value authentic food, ornate architecture, and easy rail trips to Samarkand and Bukhara. It works for those who can arrange a reliable connection and carry a backup SIM, since coworking density is thin. The relaxed pace and spacious, orderly city appeal to solo travelers and couples seeking somewhere genuinely different. It is less ideal for anyone who needs a large established international community, abundant coworking, or seamless top-tier internet, and the cold winters and hot summers mean timing matters. Choose Tashkent for exploration and value, and time your stay for spring or autumn.

sendai.costOfLiving: Sendai runs around $1600 per month for a single nomad, cheaper than Tokyo while still being a comfortable Japanese city. A furnished apartment or monthly rental in a central area typically costs $600 to $950, with short-term furnished options at the higher end and standard leases cheaper but harder to arrange short-term. Food is reasonable for Japan, and you can eat well on $350 to $500 a month by mixing supermarkets, convenience stores, and affordable local spots serving the region's specialties like gyutan grilled beef tongue. A tourist or local SIM with data runs $20 to $40 monthly. Budget $100 to $200 for a coworking membership, plus utilities, which rise in the cold winter for heating. Transport is efficient but not free, so factor in metro and train fares. Overall Sendai offers Japan's famed reliability and cleanliness at a noticeably gentler cost than the biggest cities, making it strong value by Japanese standards.
sendai.whereToWork: Sendai offers the excellent connectivity Japan is known for, with fast, reliable fixed broadband and strong mobile coverage, so you will not need a backup SIM for reliability the way you would in India, though a data SIM is still handy for getting around. Coworking spaces exist downtown around the station and central business districts, offering day passes and monthly memberships, and the quality and etiquette are high. Cafe culture is strong, with plenty of quiet, comfortable cafes and chains like the ubiquitous coffee shops where laptop work is common and outlets are often available, making cafe-based work easy and pleasant. Public wifi is available but a personal connection or SIM is more dependable. As a university city home to Tohoku University, Sendai has a studious, relaxed atmosphere well suited to focused work. For remote workers, the combination of rock-solid internet, good cafes, and central coworking makes daily productivity effortless.
sendai.gettingAround: Sendai is compact, clean, and very walkable in its center, with a grid of covered shopping arcades that make getting around pleasant in any weather. The city has two subway lines plus an extensive bus network, all punctual and easy to use with an IC card, and the loop bus is handy for sightseeing. Trains connect the center efficiently. Sendai sits on the Tohoku Shinkansen line, so Tokyo is only about 90 minutes away by bullet train, making weekend trips simple, and regional rail reaches the coast and mountains. Sendai Airport connects by a direct rail line to the city center in around 25 minutes and offers domestic flights plus some international routes. Ride-hailing exists but taxis are the usual on-demand option and are reliable if pricier than public transit. For most nomads, walking plus the subway, buses, and the occasional Shinkansen covers everything smoothly and dependably.
sendai.visas: Japan launched a digital nomad activity status in 2024, allowing eligible nationals to stay for up to six months for remote work, but it comes with conditions, notably an annual income requirement of roughly $68,000 and eligibility limited to certain countries with the right agreements, plus private health insurance coverage. It is a designated activity status rather than a long residence visa, and the six-month stay is not straightforwardly renewable, so read the criteria carefully. Many nationalities can alternatively enter Japan visa-free as tourists for stays of around 90 days, which suits shorter trips, though tourist entry is not intended for work. There is no traditional long-term nomad residence route beyond this. Because income thresholds, eligible nationalities, insurance rules, and the exact terms of the nomad status can change and are still relatively new, verify the current requirements on official Japanese immigration and embassy sources before making plans.
sendai.bestTime: Sendai enjoys four distinct seasons, and spring and autumn are the standout times to visit. Spring, particularly April, brings cherry blossoms and mild, pleasant weather ideal for exploring, while autumn from September into November offers crisp air and beautiful foliage. Summer, June through August, is warm and more humid, with a rainy season in early summer, though Sendai stays cooler and more comfortable than Tokyo or the south thanks to its northern location and coastal breezes. The city is famous for its Tanabata star festival in early August, a major draw. Winters from December through February are cold with some snow, colder than much of Japan's main population belt, so heating matters and it appeals if you like a proper winter. For the most comfortable stay with the best scenery and events, aim for spring or autumn, and consider early August if you want to experience the celebrated Tanabata festival.
sendai.prosCons: Sendai's strengths are Japan's hallmark reliability, safety, cleanliness, and excellent internet, all at a meaningfully lower cost than Tokyo, plus a compact walkable center, great food, strong public transport, and a quick 90-minute Shinkansen link to Tokyo. The new digital nomad status gives eligible high earners a legitimate route to stay six months. It is a relaxed university city with easy access to nature. The drawbacks are that it is still pricier than Asian nomad hubs, the international nomad community is small, and English can be limited outside tourist and academic circles, so a translation app helps. Winters are genuinely cold and snowy, and the six-month nomad status carries a high income bar and is not easily renewed. It is less lively than Tokyo or Osaka. Overall it is a calm, high-quality, well-run base for those who prioritize comfort, safety, and infrastructure.
sendai.whoFor: Sendai suits nomads who want the safety, reliability, and infrastructure of Japan without Tokyo's crowds and prices, and who value a calm, walkable city with quick bullet-train access to the capital. It is a strong fit for higher earners who qualify for the digital nomad status given its income requirement, or for shorter tourist-length stays. It appeals to people who love four-season climates, nature and hot springs nearby, and refined food culture including the local gyutan specialty. The university atmosphere and quiet cafes make it ideal for focused, heads-down work. It fits solo travelers and couples who prioritize comfort and quality over a big party scene or a ready-made international community. It is less suited to budget-focused nomads chasing the lowest costs, those who need a large English-speaking crowd, or anyone who dislikes cold, snowy winters, since Sendai's north climate is real.

beijing.costOfLiving: A single nomad in Beijing lands close to $1500 per month without much strain. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease inside the Third Ring, in Dongcheng, Sanlitun or Wudaokou, runs $600 to $950; shared flats and serviced studios in Chaoyang start nearer $400. Eating mostly local, at jianbing stalls, noodle shops and canteen-style Sichuan places, costs $200 to $320 a month, though a Western brunch habit adds $150 fast. A China Unicom or China Mobile SIM with 30GB to 60GB is $10 to $18. Hot-desking at a coworking space is $130 to $220; cafes are cheaper and widely tolerated. Utilities including heating, electricity and water average $40 to $80, spiking in winter. Transport is trivial: $20 to $35 covers a month of metro and buses. Value verdict: Beijing delivers a genuine world capital, superb food and near-flawless infrastructure at roughly half the cost of Tokyo or Seoul, with rent the only real pressure point.
beijing.whereToWork: Base yourself in Dongcheng near the Lama Temple and Gulou for hutong quiet with metro access, in Sanlitun or Chaoyangmen for a more international feel, or in Wudaokou if a young student-heavy scene appeals. WeWork operates several Beijing locations including Sanlitun and the CBD, and Kr Space and Ucommune run domestic-brand alternatives at lower rates. Cafe work is normal in the hutong belt around Beiluoguxiang and Wudaoying, where independent roasters keep long tables and reliable wifi; the Metal Hands and Voyage Coffee groups are dependable fixtures. Fixed broadband commonly delivers 100 to 300 Mbps and mobile 5G is fast and near-ubiquitous. The critical caveat is the Great Firewall: Google, Gmail, WhatsApp, Instagram, Slack in places, and most Western SaaS require a working VPN, and consumer VPNs degrade during political meetings. Power is stable. Cafes get loud after 2pm and rarely have plentiful sockets.
beijing.gettingAround: Beijing's metro is the workhorse: over twenty lines, signage in English, trains every two to four minutes, and fares of roughly $0.40 to $1.20 depending on distance. Buses cost about $0.15 with a transit card but are slower and less foreigner-friendly. Didi is the dominant ride-hailing app and works in English; a typical crosstown ride is $4 to $10, though rush hour traffic inside the Fourth Ring is genuinely bad. Shared bikes from Meituan and Hellobike blanket the city at around $0.20 for thirty minutes and are often the fastest option for short hops. Payment runs through Alipay or WeChat Pay, both of which now accept foreign cards. Capital Airport connects by the Airport Express for about $3.50; Daxing is further out but linked by its own express line. The city is flat and walkable block by block, but the blocks are enormous. No scooter or car is needed.
beijing.visas: China does not offer a digital nomad visa, and remote work on a tourist entry is technically outside the visa's purpose. As of 2026, citizens of a long list of countries including most of the EU, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea can enter visa-free for up to 30 days for tourism, business and family visits, a scheme repeatedly extended and expanded since 2024. United States and Canadian passport holders are not on that list and still need a visa: the standard L tourist visa is usually issued for 30 or 60 days per entry, often with ten-year multiple-entry validity for Americans. Separately, the 240-hour visa-free transit policy allows stays of up to ten days for travellers continuing to a third country through Beijing and most major ports. Extensions of 30 days are possible at the Public Security Bureau exit-entry office but are discretionary. Register your address with local police within 24 hours of arrival.
beijing.bestTime: Beijing has a sharply continental climate with four unmistakable seasons. September and October are the clear best window: dry, blue, with highs around 22C to 26C and the golden light that makes the Fragrant Hills and the Great Wall worth the trip. April and May are the second choice, pleasant but punctuated by spring dust storms blowing in from the north. June through August are hot and humid, peaking near 35C, with the bulk of the annual rain arriving in July and August as short violent downpours. Winter, from December to February, is dry, bright and bitterly cold, with lows near minus 10C and the worst air-quality episodes when coal heating and still air combine, though pollution has improved markedly since the 2010s. Chinese New Year, falling in late January or February, shuts much of the city and makes domestic travel chaotic. Mid-Autumn Festival and the October National Day week also crowd every attraction.
beijing.prosCons: The strengths are substantial. Beijing is one of the great historical capitals, with the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Great Wall within reach, backed by an art scene at 798 and a hutong bar and coffee culture that rewards long stays. Infrastructure is exceptional: a vast cheap metro, fast trains to Shanghai and Xi'an, sub-second mobile payments, delivery of anything within an hour, and personal safety at a level few world cities match. Food, from imperial to Uyghur to Sichuan, is world class and cheap. Against that, the internet is the dealbreaker for many: the Great Firewall makes routine Western tools dependent on a VPN that can and does fail at politically sensitive moments. Winter air quality still has bad days, winters are punishing, and the language barrier is real, since English is far less widespread than in Southeast Asia. The nomad community is thin and bureaucracy for foreigners is heavy.
beijing.whoFor: Beijing suits the nomad who wants depth rather than convenience: someone with an interest in Chinese history, language or business, a tolerance for bureaucracy, and work that survives a VPN-mediated internet connection. It rewards long stays, learners of Mandarin, and people whose income is high enough that a $700 flat and $3 metro days feel like an obvious bargain against Tokyo or Singapore. Journalists, researchers, supply-chain and manufacturing consultants, and anyone building China-facing product will find the city indispensable. It fits poorly for those who need Google Workspace, Slack and Zoom to work without friction every single hour, for social nomads seeking a ready-made expat coworking scene of the Chiang Mai or Lisbon variety, and for anyone chasing beaches, warmth or year-round outdoor living. Travellers who dislike cold winters, heavy air-pollution days, or navigating daily life in a language they cannot read should look elsewhere in Asia.

shanghai.costOfLiving: Shanghai is China's most expensive city and $1800 per month is a realistic single-person figure rather than a generous one. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in the former French Concession, Jing'an or Xuhui costs $750 to $1200; move out to Hongkou, Yangpu or beyond the Inner Ring and $500 to $700 buys the same space. Food splits sharply: local noodle shops, dumpling joints and canteens keep monthly spend near $250, while the international restaurant scene that makes Shanghai famous can double it. A data SIM with 30GB or more runs $10 to $18. Coworking hot desks are $150 to $280, the highest in mainland China. Utilities average $45 to $90, with summer air-conditioning and winter heating the swing factors. Metro and Didi together come to $30 to $50. Value verdict: costs are high by Chinese standards and modest by global ones, and Shanghai buys more genuine urban quality per dollar than any comparable city in East Asia.
shanghai.whereToWork: The former French Concession is the default base, walkable and plane-tree shaded, with Jing'an offering a more polished version and Xuhui a quieter one. Coworking is mature here: WeWork holds numerous Shanghai buildings, Distrii and Kr Space run large domestic networks, and Naked Hub sites were absorbed into WeWork's portfolio. Independent cafe work is easy and accepted; the Seesaw and Manner chains are ubiquitous, and specialty roasters cluster around Anfu Lu, Yongkang Lu and Wukang Lu. Fibre broadband typically runs 200 to 500 Mbps and 5G coverage is excellent throughout the inner districts. The Great Firewall applies as it does nationwide, so a functioning VPN is a prerequisite for Google, Slack, WhatsApp and most Western SaaS, and reliability dips during major political events. Power supply is stable. The practical caveats are noise and seating: popular cafes are packed on weekends and sockets are scarce, so arrive before eleven.
shanghai.gettingAround: Shanghai's metro is among the world's largest, with twenty-plus lines, bilingual signage and fares of about $0.40 to $1.30. Buses cost around $0.30 but are slower. Didi handles ride-hailing; a typical inner-city trip is $4 to $12 and the app works in English with foreign cards linked through Alipay or WeChat Pay. Shared bikes from Meituan and Hellobike cost roughly $0.20 per half hour and suit the flat, dense inner districts perfectly. Shanghai is the most genuinely walkable major city in China, especially the French Concession, where the street grid is human-scaled. Pudong Airport connects by metro Line 2 for about $1 or by the Maglev in eight minutes for around $7; Hongqiao is on Lines 2 and 10 and doubles as the high-speed rail hub, putting Hangzhou within 50 minutes and Beijing within four and a half hours. No scooter or car is required.
shanghai.visas: China has no digital nomad visa and none is planned as of 2026, so remote work here happens on tourist or business entries. Passport holders from most EU states, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea can enter visa-free for up to 30 days under the unilateral scheme China expanded through 2024 and 2025. American and Canadian citizens remain excluded and need a standard L tourist visa, typically valid for 30 or 60 day stays, often on a ten-year multiple-entry sticker for US applicants. Shanghai is also a designated port for the 240-hour visa-free transit policy, which permits stays of up to ten days when continuing to a third country, a route many use to add a Shanghai leg between two other destinations. A single 30-day extension can be requested at the municipal exit-entry administration but approval is discretionary. Hotels register guests automatically; anyone in private accommodation must register at the local police station within 24 hours.
shanghai.bestTime: Shanghai is humid subtropical, and the shoulder seasons are the reason to come. October and early November are the standout window: dry, clear, highs near 22C, low humidity. Late March through May is nearly as good, though April and early June bring persistent drizzle. June and July deliver the meiyu plum rains, weeks of grey, sticky, near-constant humidity that locals dread more than the heat. July and August are the peak of summer, with highs above 35C, high humidity and typhoon risk that runs from July into September, occasionally closing the airport and flooding low streets. Winter, December to February, is not freezing but is damp, grey and poorly heated indoors, and feels colder than the 4C to 8C readings suggest. Chinese New Year empties the city for about a week and reopens it slowly. The Shanghai International Film Festival in June and the November import expo crowd hotels.
shanghai.prosCons: Shanghai is the most livable large city in mainland China for a foreigner. The former French Concession offers tree-lined walkability that almost nowhere in Asia matches, the food scene spans street dumplings to genuinely world-class restaurants, the metro is vast and cheap, and personal safety is excellent at any hour. English is more widely spoken here than anywhere else in China, the international community is large and long-established, high-speed rail puts half the country within a day, and infrastructure from mobile payments to same-hour delivery simply works. The drawbacks are equally clear. Costs are the highest in the country and rents in the desirable inner districts have risen steadily. The Great Firewall still gates every Western work tool behind a VPN that can fail without warning. Summer is oppressively humid with typhoon disruption, winter is damp and badly heated, air quality has bad days, and the visa framework caps most visits at 30 to 60 days.
shanghai.whoFor: Shanghai fits the nomad who wants a serious, fully functioning global city rather than a cheap one: high earners, consultants and founders with China-facing business, finance and design professionals, and anyone who values walkable streets, restaurant depth and an international social scene over a low burn rate. It is also the softest landing in China for a first visit, since English goes further and the expat infrastructure is decades old. Mandarin learners get a diverse, tolerant environment, though Beijing offers cleaner standard pronunciation. It suits poorly the budget nomad, since $1800 buys markedly more in Chiang Mai, Hanoi or Tbilisi, and anyone whose workflow depends on uninterrupted access to Google, Slack or Zoom without a VPN should think hard. Nomads chasing long visa runways, tropical weather, beaches or an outdoor lifestyle will find the 30-day tourist cap and the muggy summers frustrating.

xiamen.costOfLiving: Xiamen supports a comfortable single-person month at about $1200. Furnished monthly rentals on Xiamen Island, in Siming district near Zhongshan Road or the university, run $350 to $600 for a one-bedroom, and sea-view apartments in the newer Huli towers sit at the top of that band; mainland-side Jimei and Haicang drop to $250 to $350. Food is a highlight and a bargain: local seafood, satay noodles and Hokkien snacks keep monthly eating near $180 to $280. A 30GB SIM costs $10 to $18. Coworking desks are $90 to $170, well below the tier-one cities. Utilities average $35 to $70, driven mainly by summer air-conditioning. Metro, bus and BRT together cost $15 to $25 a month. Value verdict: Xiamen is one of the best cost-to-quality trades in coastal China, offering clean air, a subtropical waterfront and tier-one infrastructure at roughly two-thirds of Shanghai's price.
xiamen.whereToWork: Base on Xiamen Island. Siming district puts you near the seafront ring road, Zhongshan Road's old shophouses and Xiamen University; the Shapowei and Zengcuoan areas draw a younger, creative crowd with a dense cluster of independent cafes. Huli is newer, more corporate and closer to the airport. The city's coffee culture is unusually strong for a second-tier Chinese city, and cafe work in Shapowei or around Baicheng Beach is straightforward, though most independents are small and seating is limited. Coworking exists through domestic operators and the Software Park II and III campuses in Siming, which host a real tech workforce and serviced offices at reasonable rates. Broadband commonly delivers 100 to 300 Mbps and 5G coverage is comprehensive across the island. The nationwide firewall applies, so a VPN is essential for Western tools. Power is reliable. Typhoon season can bring occasional outages and closures in late summer.
xiamen.gettingAround: Xiamen has a growing metro network, with Lines 1, 2 and 3 covering the island and the mainland districts and fares of about $0.30 to $1. Line 1 crosses the sea on a causeway, which is a genuinely scenic commute. Buses cost around $0.15 and the BRT elevated busway is fast across the island. Didi is the ride-hailing standard, with typical island trips at $3 to $8. Shared bikes are everywhere at roughly $0.20 per half hour, and Xiamen is one of the better Chinese cities for cycling thanks to the seafront path and a dedicated elevated bike skyway. The island core is genuinely walkable and pleasant on foot. Gaoqi International Airport sits on the island itself, only fifteen minutes from Siming by taxi at around $6. High-speed rail links Fuzhou in about ninety minutes and Shenzhen in three and a half hours. No scooter or car is needed; electric scooters are in fact restricted on the island.
xiamen.visas: The rules are national, so Xiamen follows the same framework as Beijing and Shanghai. There is no Chinese digital nomad visa. Citizens of most EU countries, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea can enter visa-free for stays of up to 30 days under the scheme China has progressively widened since late 2023. US and Canadian passport holders are not covered and must obtain an L tourist visa in advance, generally permitting 30 or 60 days per entry, with long multiple-entry validity common for Americans. Xiamen Gaoqi is a designated port for the 240-hour visa-free transit policy, allowing up to ten days when travelling onward to a third country, which suits a short island stopover well. A 30-day extension may be requested from the Xiamen exit-entry bureau but is granted at the officer's discretion. Police registration within 24 hours applies to anyone not staying in a hotel.
xiamen.bestTime: Xiamen is subtropical and mild, with a comfortable stretch that is longer than most of China's. October to December is the best window: dry, sunny, highs of 22C to 28C and low humidity, ideal for the seafront and for day trips to the Fujian tulou earth buildings. March to May is warm and pleasant but increasingly humid, with spring sea fog common. June through September is hot and sticky, regularly above 32C with high humidity, and this is also typhoon season; Fujian takes direct hits most years, and a serious storm can close the airport and shut the city for a day or two. Rainfall peaks between May and August. January and February are the coolest months, around 12C to 18C, damp but rarely cold. Chinese New Year fills Gulangyu island and the seafront with domestic tourists, as do the May and October national holiday weeks.
xiamen.prosCons: Xiamen is widely rated one of China's most liveable cities and the reasons hold up. The air is clean by mainland standards, the island is compact, green and edged by a continuous seafront promenade and bike skyway, and the climate is mild for most of the year. Seafood and Hokkien cuisine are excellent and cheap, the metro and airport are modern, Gulangyu island and the Fujian tulou are on the doorstep, and the pace is markedly calmer than Shanghai or Shenzhen while the infrastructure is barely worse. Costs sit around two-thirds of tier-one levels. The drawbacks start with isolation: the foreign community is small, English is much less common than in Shanghai, and there is no established nomad scene, so a Mandarin base or high tolerance for solitude matters. The firewall applies in full, coworking options are limited compared with tier-one cities, typhoons disrupt late summer, and domestic tourist crowds swamp the main sights during national holidays.
xiamen.whoFor: Xiamen suits the self-sufficient nomad who wants a coastal Chinese city with real quality of life and does not need a ready-made expat network: solo workers with steady clients, Mandarin learners looking for a calmer environment than Beijing, cyclists and runners drawn to the seafront, and anyone burnt out on megacity density but unwilling to give up fast trains, cheap metro and same-day delivery. It is a strong second or third China destination for someone who has already learned how the country works. It is a poor fit for beginners who need English signage and hand-holding, for social nomads who want coworking friends and meetups on tap, and for anyone whose job cannot tolerate VPN-dependent access to Western tools. Those needing long visa runways will also find the 30-day ceiling restrictive, and travellers sensitive to humidity should avoid the June to September window entirely.

guilin.costOfLiving: Guilin is genuinely cheap and $900 per month buys a comfortable single life. Furnished monthly rentals in the city centre near Zhengyang pedestrian street or the Two Rivers and Four Lakes area run $200 to $380 for a one-bedroom; Yangshuo, an hour south and the more scenic base, sits at $250 to $450 for a guesthouse room or small flat with a karst view. Food is inexpensive, with Guilin rice noodles at under $2 a bowl keeping monthly eating to $150 to $230. A data SIM is $10 to $18. Formal coworking barely exists here, so budget $0 to $80 for cafe spend or a desk in a Yangshuo guesthouse. Utilities average $30 to $60. Local transport is $10 to $20 a month. Value verdict: among the lowest costs available in a Chinese city with modern infrastructure, and the landscape is the compensation for the thinner urban amenities.
guilin.whereToWork: Guilin city is the practical base for infrastructure, with the area around the Lijiang riverbank and Zhengyang Road offering hotels, apartments and a reasonable cafe scene. Many long-stayers prefer Yangshuo, an hour away by high-speed rail, where West Street has decades of backpacker infrastructure and the surrounding villages of Jima and Gaotian offer riverside guesthouses with desks and terraces. Dedicated coworking is essentially absent in both; work happens in cafes, guesthouse lobbies and hotel business centres. Broadband is generally solid at 50 to 200 Mbps in the city and more variable in rural Yangshuo, where a good 5G plan and a mobile hotspot are the sensible backup. Coverage across the karst valleys is better than expected but has dead spots. The national firewall applies, so a working VPN is mandatory. Power is generally reliable but rural outages happen during heavy summer storms. Cafes are quiet outside tourist peaks.
guilin.gettingAround: Guilin has no metro. City buses cover the centre at roughly $0.15 to $0.30 a ride and are the local default. Didi works throughout and is the practical choice for most trips, with typical city fares of $2 to $6; taxis are similarly cheap. Shared bikes and shared e-bikes are available in the city, and in Yangshuo renting an electric scooter for around $8 to $12 a day is the standard way to reach the villages, rice terraces and climbing crags, since the countryside is spread out and buses are infrequent. Guilin is flat and walkable in its centre, and the lakeside paths are pleasant. High-speed rail is the strong point: Yangshuo is under 30 minutes and Guangzhou around two and a half hours from Guilin West. Liangjiang International Airport lies 30 kilometres out, connected by an airport bus for about $3 or a $15 taxi. A scooter is genuinely useful in Yangshuo, unnecessary in the city.
guilin.visas: National Chinese rules apply, and there is no digital nomad visa. Most EU, UK, Australian, New Zealand, Japanese and Korean passport holders can enter mainland China visa-free for up to 30 days under the expanded unilateral scheme; US and Canadian citizens still need an L tourist visa, usually issued for 30 or 60 day stays. Guangxi province has an additional regional feature worth knowing: a visa-free arrangement exists for ASEAN tour groups entering Guilin, but it applies to organised groups, not independent Western travellers, so it is not a workaround. The 240-hour visa-free transit policy covers designated ports, and travellers commonly enter through Guangzhou, Shenzhen or Shanghai and reach Guilin by high-speed rail within that window. Extensions of 30 days can be applied for at the Guilin exit-entry bureau, though smaller-city offices tend to be slower. Police registration within 24 hours is required for anyone not in a hotel.
guilin.bestTime: Guilin is subtropical with a long humid summer. April to June is when the karst landscape looks best, green and misty, but it is also the wettest stretch, with May the peak rainfall month and occasional flooding along the Li River. The most comfortable window is late September to November: warm days around 22C to 28C, far less rain, clear enough for the Longji rice terraces, which are golden in late September and October before harvest. July and August are hot at 33C to 35C, humid, stormy and crowded with domestic tourists on school holidays. December to February is cool, damp and often grey, with temperatures of 8C to 14C, misty in a way that photographers love and everyone else finds bleak; the Li River cruise still runs but views can vanish. Chinese New Year and the May and October golden weeks bring heavy domestic crowds to Yangshuo and the terraces.
guilin.prosCons: The landscape is the whole argument and it is a strong one. The karst hills along the Li River and around Yangshuo are among the most striking scenery in Asia, with world-class rock climbing, cycling through rice fields, bamboo rafting and the Longji terraces a few hours north. Costs are very low even by Chinese standards, food is cheap and distinctive, high-speed rail links the region efficiently, and Yangshuo has a decades-old backpacker infrastructure that means more English and more foreigner-friendly guesthouses than a city of this size would normally offer. The drawbacks are structural. There is no real coworking, no professional community and no nomad scene beyond climbers and travellers passing through. Guilin city itself is unremarkable and heavily geared to domestic tour groups, whose crowds and hard selling can wear thin. Summers are hot, wet and stormy, winters grey. The firewall applies, medical and international services are limited, and the 30-day visa ceiling caps any real settling in.
guilin.whoFor: Guilin and Yangshuo fit the outdoor-minded nomad on a modest budget: rock climbers above all, since Yangshuo is one of the world's great sport-climbing destinations, plus cyclists, runners, photographers and writers who want low costs and dramatic scenery over urban amenities. It rewards short, focused stays of a few weeks where the work is solitary and the reward is the countryside, and it suits travellers already comfortable in China who can handle limited English outside the tourist strip. It is wrong for anyone who needs coworking, a professional network or reliable in-person meetings, for nomads who want nightlife, restaurant variety or a large international community, and for anyone with heavy bandwidth demands in rural accommodation. Those who dislike heat, humidity, heavy rain or tour-group crowds should avoid the summer entirely, and anyone seeking a long-term base will run into the visa limits quickly.

newdelhi.costOfLiving: New Delhi runs comfortably at $900 per month for a single nomad, and can be done for far less. A furnished monthly rental in a good central-south neighbourhood such as Hauz Khas, Safdarjung Enclave, Saket or Greater Kailash costs $300 to $550 for a one-bedroom; barsati rooftop rooms and serviced studios start nearer $200, while Lutyens' Delhi and Vasant Vihar climb well past $800. Food is very cheap: local thalis, street food and home delivery keep monthly eating at $120 to $220, with restaurant meals in Khan Market or Aerocity at $12 to $25 pushing that higher. A Jio or Airtel SIM with generous data is $5 to $10, among the cheapest in the world. Coworking hot desks run $70 to $160. Utilities are $40 to $90, with summer air-conditioning the dominant cost. Metro and cabs total $25 to $50. Value verdict: exceptional purchasing power, with air quality rather than money the real tax on living here.
newdelhi.whereToWork: South Delhi is the sensible base. Hauz Khas and its village, Saket, Greater Kailash and Shahpur Jat combine cafes, metro access and residential calm; Gurugram, technically in Haryana, holds the densest concentration of corporate coworking. WeWork, Awfis, 91springboard, Innov8 and IndiQube all operate multiple Delhi and Gurugram locations, with Awfis and 91springboard the best value. Cafe work is well established at Blue Tokai Coffee Roasters, which has numerous Delhi outlets and reliable wifi, and at the cafes around Hauz Khas Village and Champa Gali in Saidulajab, a converted lane of studios and coffee shops built for exactly this. Fibre broadband from Jio or Airtel delivers 100 to 300 Mbps cheaply and 4G and 5G are fast and inexpensive, so a hotspot is a viable primary connection. No VPN is needed. Power cuts are shorter than they once were but inverters or backup are worth confirming with any landlord, especially in summer.
newdelhi.gettingAround: The Delhi Metro is the best in India: clean, air-conditioned, extensive, with fares of about $0.15 to $0.75 and a contactless card or the DMRC app for entry. It is the fastest way across a city where road traffic is severe. Uber and Ola both operate, and Rapido offers cheap motorbike taxis; a typical car ride across South Delhi is $2 to $6, an auto-rickshaw the same trip $1.50 to $4, best booked through an app to avoid meter arguments. Walkability is poor in most areas: footpaths are broken or absent, distances are large and summer heat and winter smog discourage it, though Lodhi Gardens, Khan Market and Hauz Khas are pleasant on foot. Indira Gandhi International Airport connects via the Airport Express in about twenty minutes to New Delhi station for roughly $0.70. Rail from Nizamuddin and New Delhi stations reaches Jaipur and Agra in a few hours. No scooter or car is necessary.
newdelhi.visas: India offers no digital nomad visa as of 2026, and remote work is done on a tourist entry. The e-Tourist visa is the standard route and is granted online to citizens of most Western countries, typically in 30-day, one-year and five-year variants; the one-year and five-year versions allow multiple entries with a maximum continuous stay of 90 days for most nationalities, extended to 180 days per visit for US, UK, Canadian and Japanese passport holders. Apply only through the official indianvisaonline government portal, since numerous lookalike sites charge inflated fees. Tourist visas cannot generally be extended inside India; the expected pattern is to exit and re-enter, and while the old 60-day re-entry gap was removed years ago, immigration officers still scrutinise back-to-back tourist stays. Employment in India requires a separate business or employment visa. Protected Area Permits apply to parts of the northeast, Ladakh and the Andamans, none of which affect Delhi itself.
newdelhi.bestTime: Delhi's year has one clearly good stretch and several difficult ones. October to March is the season, with the sweet spot from late October to early December and again in February and March: dry, sunny, highs of 20C to 28C. Deep winter, late December and January, is cool at 5C to 18C and afflicted by dense fog that delays flights and trains, compounded by the city's worst air pollution, which peaks after Diwali as crop stubble burning coincides with cold stagnant air. April and May are punishingly hot, regularly above 40C and touching 45C, with hot loo winds. The southwest monsoon arrives around late June and runs through September, breaking the heat but bringing humidity, flooding and waterlogged roads. Holi falls in March, Diwali in October or November, and Durga Puja and Dussehra in the autumn; all are worth planning around, and the air after Diwali is the single biggest reason to avoid November.
newdelhi.prosCons: Delhi delivers enormous value and depth. The cost of living is extremely low relative to the quality of housing, food and coworking available, mobile data is world-beating in price and speed, no firewall or VPN complicates work, and English is widely spoken in professional and urban settings, making daily life far easier than in China. The metro is excellent, the coworking sector is mature and competitive, and the historical layers, from Mughal tombs to Lutyens' avenues, are extraordinary. Rail and cheap flights open the whole subcontinent. The overwhelming drawback is air quality: winter pollution in Delhi routinely reaches hazardous levels and represents a genuine health cost, not an inconvenience. Summer heat above 45C is dangerous, monsoon flooding disrupts the city, traffic and noise are relentless, and walkability is poor. Women travellers consistently report Delhi as less comfortable than southern Indian cities. Bureaucracy, scams targeting new arrivals, and inconsistent power and water in cheaper housing add friction.
newdelhi.whoFor: New Delhi fits the nomad who wants maximum purchasing power in a large, English-functional city with real professional infrastructure: founders and freelancers working with Indian teams, journalists and researchers, consultants in tech or development, and long-haul travellers using the capital as a base for the subcontinent. It rewards those who plan around the calendar, arriving in October or February and leaving before the November smog and the May heat. Budget-conscious workers who want a $400 flat, $8 monthly data and $100 coworking will find few equivalents anywhere. It is a poor fit for anyone with asthma, allergies or respiratory sensitivity, for whom Delhi's winter air is disqualifying, and for nomads who prioritise walkability, clean air, quiet or outdoor exercise. Those seeking a gentler Indian introduction should consider Bengaluru, Goa or Pondicherry; those wanting a beach or mountain lifestyle will be happier in Rishikesh, Dharamshala or the coast.

dhaka.costOfLiving: A single nomad can live in Dhaka on roughly $700 per month, and that figure buys a comfortable rather than a bare existence. A furnished one-bedroom flat on a monthly basis in Gulshan, Banani or Dhanmondi runs $300 to $500, while comparable space in Mohammadpur or Uttara drops to $180 to $300. Local meals cost $1 to $3, a plate of biryani at a neighbourhood institution is around $2.50, and restaurant dining in the diplomatic zone climbs to $10 to $20 per head. A Grameenphone or Robi SIM with 30GB to 50GB costs $4 to $8 monthly. Coworking desks run $60 to $120. Utilities including electricity, an inverter or generator share and a fibre line total $40 to $80, higher in summer when air conditioning runs constantly. Transport rarely exceeds $40. The value is genuine, though comfort here is bought in air conditioning, filtered air and backup power rather than in square metres.
dhaka.whereToWork: Base yourself in Gulshan, Banani or Dhanmondi; these hold the embassies, the reliable fibre and most of the cafe culture. Moar and North End Coffee Roasters have branches across Gulshan and Dhanmondi and are the default laptop cafes, with Crimson Cup and Cafe Mango also tolerating long sessions. For dedicated space, Impact Hub Dhaka and Hubdhaka in Gulshan offer day passes and monthly desks, and Bangladesh has a growing cluster of startup incubators around Gulshan Avenue that rent desks. Fibre to residential and office buildings commonly delivers 30 Mbps to 100 Mbps and is decent by regional standards, but load shedding remains a real constraint, so confirm any building has an IPS, inverter or generator before signing. Mobile 4G is widely usable as backup. Cafes get loud in the evening, power sockets are scarce in older venues, and the government has previously throttled mobile internet during unrest, so a VPN and a data buffer are sensible.
dhaka.gettingAround: Dhaka has no comprehensive metro, but Line 6 of the Dhaka Metro Rail now runs elevated from Uttara North through Mirpur, Farmgate and Motijheel, and it is transformative for that corridor; fares are roughly $0.20 to $1.00. Everything else is road, and Dhaka has some of the worst congestion on earth, with average speeds in the single digits during peak hours. Pathao and Uber are the workhorses: a Pathao motorcycle ride across town costs $1 to $3 and is far faster than a car, while a car booking is $3 to $8. CNG auto-rickshaws cost $1.50 to $4 after the inevitable haggling. Local buses are cheap at under $0.30 but crowded and hard to parse without Bangla. Walkability is poor because footpaths are broken, occupied or missing. Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport sits north of the city; allow ninety minutes from Gulshan by car despite the short distance. No scooter or car ownership is needed.
dhaka.visas: Bangladesh has no digital nomad visa and none is under serious discussion. Most Western nationals, including US, UK, EU, Canadian and Australian passport holders, are eligible for visa on arrival at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport for up to 30 days at a fee of around $51, but this is discretionary rather than guaranteed: immigration officers can and do refuse it, and they typically expect proof of onward travel, a hotel booking and sufficient cash. The safer route is applying in advance at a Bangladeshi mission for a tourist visa, which is commonly issued for 30 to 90 days and sometimes with multiple entries and validity up to a year. Extensions are handled by the Department of Immigration and Passports in Agargaon, are bureaucratic and are usually granted only for short periods. Overstays attract fines and departure delays. Working remotely on a tourist visa is not formally provided for; the on-the-ground reality is that laptop work goes unremarked.
dhaka.bestTime: The comfortable window is November to February, when daytime highs settle around 25C to 29C, humidity drops and evenings turn genuinely cool in December and January. That is the season for travel and for the winter wedding and cultural calendar. March and April heat up quickly, and by April and May temperatures reach the high thirties with brutal humidity and pre-monsoon nor'wester storms. The southwest monsoon runs roughly June to September, delivering heavy, sustained rain, waterlogged streets and serious traffic paralysis, though it is also the greenest and cheapest stretch. October is a transitional month and increasingly pleasant late on. The offsetting problem with the cool season is air quality: Dhaka regularly ranks among the world's most polluted cities from December through March, with brick kiln smoke and dust pushing AQI past 200. Key dates include Pohela Boishakh in mid-April, Durga Puja in autumn and the two Eid holidays, which empty the city.
dhaka.prosCons: The case for Dhaka is cost, energy and access. Very few capitals let a remote worker live centrally, eat well and hire help on $700 a month, and the country is genuinely cheap once rent is settled. English is widely spoken in the professional and educated classes, hospitality toward foreigners is warm and often disarming, the food culture is underrated, and Dhaka is a serious base for exploring Sylhet's tea hills, the Sundarbans and Cox's Bazar. The startup and NGO scene means there are actual peers. Against that: the traffic is genuinely among the world's worst and eats hours daily, the air quality in winter is a real health cost rather than an inconvenience, footpaths and public space are poor, and load shedding still interrupts work. Political unrest and hartals can shut the city and disrupt internet. Solo women face persistent staring and harassment, alcohol is restricted, serious medical care means flying to Bangkok, and there is close to no nomad infrastructure.
dhaka.whoFor: Dhaka suits the nomad with a purpose beyond arbitrage: development sector workers, researchers, journalists, textile and supply chain people, and anyone with family, business or a genuine curiosity about South Asia at full volume. It rewards travellers who have already done India or Pakistan, who are comfortable negotiating chaos, and who value cost and human warmth over infrastructure. Founders on a tight runway can extend it dramatically here. It is a poor fit for first-time nomads, for anyone with asthma, allergies or cardiovascular issues given the winter air, and for people who need walkable streets, reliable power, an established coworking community or an easy social scene of other remote workers. Anyone whose priority list includes nightlife, beaches within reach, or predictable calendars will be frustrated. Solo women should weigh the harassment reality honestly. Those wanting cheap Asia without the friction should look at Chiang Mai, Da Nang or Kathmandu instead.

islamabad.costOfLiving: Islamabad is Pakistan's most expensive city and also its most liveable, and $800 a month covers a single nomad comfortably. A furnished one-bedroom or studio on a monthly lease in F-6, F-7, F-8 or E-11 runs $250 to $450, with G-sectors and Bahria Town cheaper at $150 to $280; serviced apartments aimed at expats climb past $600. Local food is very cheap, with a plate of nihari or karahi at $2 to $4 and street food under $1, while Western style restaurants in the F-6 Super Market or Kohsar Market area cost $8 to $18. A Jazz or Zong SIM with a generous monthly data bundle costs $5 to $10. Coworking desks are $70 to $130. Utilities including electricity, gas and a fibre line run $50 to $100, spiking in summer with air conditioning. Transport is $30 to $60 on ride-hailing. The value is strong: clean air, greenery and space for far less than comparable Asian capitals.
islamabad.whereToWork: Base yourself in the F-6, F-7, F-8, F-11 or E-11 sectors; they are leafy, low-rise and close to the markets and cafes. Kohsar Market and F-6 Super Market are the cafe cores, with Chai Khana, Burning Brownie, Mocca Coffee and the various branches of Gloria Jean's and Second Cup all workable, and Monal and the Pir Sohawa road offering views rather than productivity. For dedicated space, the National Incubation Center at NUST, Daftarkhwan and Colabs have Islamabad operations, and Blue Area holds most of the serious office coworking stock. Fibre from Nayatel or StormFiber commonly delivers 50 Mbps to 200 Mbps and is genuinely reliable, which is the city's quiet advantage. The caveats: load shedding is milder here than in Karachi or Lahore but still occurs, so verify a UPS or generator; mobile internet is periodically throttled or suspended during protests, so a paid VPN is effectively mandatory; and cafes close early.
islamabad.gettingAround: There is no metro in the underground sense, but the Islamabad-Rawalpindi Metrobus runs a dedicated corridor from Saddar in Rawalpindi to Pak Secretariat, with a separate line out to the airport, and fares are about $0.10 to $0.15. Beyond that, ride-hailing dominates: Careem, InDrive and Yango cover the city, with a typical cross-sector car ride at $1.50 to $4 and a bike ride at $0.60 to $1.50. Traditional taxis and Suzuki vans exist but are not worth the negotiation. Islamabad is unusually spacious, laid out on a numbered sector grid with wide roads and good greenery, but the sectors are large and distances long, so it is pleasant to walk within a sector and impractical between them. Islamabad International Airport is roughly 25km southwest; expect $8 to $15 by Careem or 45 minutes on the airport Metrobus. A car is not needed, though it helps for weekend trips toward Murree, Swat and the north.
islamabad.visas: Pakistan runs an online e-visa system through the NADRA portal, and it is the standard route for Western nationals. Tourist e-visas are commonly granted for 30 to 90 days, and citizens of a long list of countries including the US, UK, most of the EU, Canada and Australia can apply fully online without a sponsor or letter of invitation; processing typically takes days to a few weeks and fees vary by nationality, often $30 to $60. Pakistan does not have a digital nomad visa despite periodic press speculation, so do not plan around one. Extensions are applied for through the same online portal and are sometimes granted, though outcomes are inconsistent and best started well before expiry. Business visas are available with an invitation from a registered Pakistani company. The important gotchas are regional rather than bureaucratic: some areas require a No Objection Certificate for travel, notably parts of Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's border districts and Azad Kashmir. Overstaying is treated seriously.
islamabad.bestTime: Islamabad's climate is one of its best arguments, with four real seasons rather than a wet and dry binary. March and April are the peak, with highs in the low twenties, blossom across the sectors and hiking weather on the Margalla Hills trails. May and June are hot and dry, regularly hitting 38C to 40C, and this is the window when the Margallas become unpleasant by midday. The monsoon lands roughly July through mid-September, bringing violent thunderstorms, spectacular skies, humidity and occasional flash flooding on the nullahs, though it also greens the hills. Late September through November is the second excellent window: dry, mild and clear, and the season for heading north to Hunza and Skardu before the passes close. December to February is genuinely cold, dropping near freezing at night, with fog and a smog season that is real though far milder than Lahore's. Pakistan Day in March and both Eids anchor the calendar.
islamabad.prosCons: Islamabad is the anomaly in South Asia: a planned, green, low-density capital backed onto the forested Margalla Hills, with clean air by regional standards, wide roads, functional fibre, cheap ride-hailing and almost none of the density or noise of Karachi, Lahore or Delhi. Food is excellent and very cheap, the people are famously hospitable, and the city is the gateway to the Karakoram, arguably the best mountain trekking on the planet, with Hunza and Skardu a short flight or long drive away. The costs are considerable. It is quiet to the point of dullness, with an early-closing, largely alcohol-free social life and no nomad scene to speak of. Internet shutdowns and platform blocks during political tension are routine and can genuinely disrupt work. Security requires ongoing attention, with periodic incidents in the wider region and hard restrictions on travel to some provinces. Bureaucracy is heavy, distances are car-dependent, and solo women face real cultural friction.
islamabad.whoFor: Islamabad fits the self-directed remote worker who wants mountains within reach, a low burn rate and clean air, and who does not need a scene to be productive. Trekkers, climbers, motorcyclists and photographers get outsized value because the city is a comfortable, well-connected base camp for the Karakoram and Hindu Kush. It also suits people with Pakistani family or business ties, and those already working with the country's fast-growing outsourcing and startup sector. Long-stay travellers who value order and greenery over stimulation will be surprised at how well it works. Skip it if a bar culture, an existing nomad community or a dense walkable core matters, if your work cannot tolerate occasional internet suspensions, or if you want a low-friction visa reset ecosystem. Solo women, LGBT nomads and anyone who needs to be visibly unconventional should weigh the social conservatism seriously. Party-oriented or first-time nomads will be much happier in Southeast Asia.

male.costOfLiving: Malé is expensive, small and imports nearly everything, and $2,200 a month is a realistic single-person figure that still requires care.
