It rewards curiosity and patience, and it punishes anyone hoping for a straightforward, cheap, easy base. It works well for people who want a compact, walkable city with world-class food and history at the door, and who can absorb the cost. It is a poor fit for anyone seeking a large nomad community, cheap living, beach access or political calm; Tel Aviv answers most of those better and is very close. Anyone considering it should check their own government's travel advice for the region before booking, and should understand that conditions here can change quickly.

ankara.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $880 a month as a solo remote worker in Ankara, which makes it appreciably cheaper than Istanbul for a similar standard of city living. A one-bedroom apartment in Cankaya, Kizilay or Bahcelievler runs about $300 to $450, and the newer districts out towards Cayyolu cost about the same for more space and a longer commute. Groceries land around $180 to $250, helped by neighbourhood pazar markets that undercut supermarkets on produce by a wide margin. A lunch of doner or pide is $3 to $5, a proper restaurant dinner with drinks $15 to $25, and a monthly transit pass about $25. Utilities run $60 to $110 and spike in winter, when Ankara's continental climate makes heating a real line item rather than an afterthought.
ankara.whereToWork: Ankara is a government and university city rather than a tourist one, and its working spaces reflect that. Coworking clusters around Kizilay, Cankaya and the technology parks attached to METU and Bilkent, where rates run about $90 to $150 a month and the other members are more likely to be Turkish founders and engineers than visiting nomads. Cafe culture is strong and laptop-friendly, particularly in the student areas around Bahcelievler and Tunali Hilmi, and third-wave coffee has arrived properly in the last few years. Fixed-line internet is fast and cheap, and mobile data is good, though foreign SIM cards get throttled after 120 days unless the handset is registered, which is a well-known and expensive piece of Turkish bureaucracy worth planning around.
ankara.gettingAround: Ankara has a metro with four lines plus the older Ankaray light rail, and between them they cover the spine of the city from Kizilay outwards. Buses and shared dolmus minibuses fill everything else, and an Ankarakart smart card pays for all of it at roughly $0.40 a ride. The city is spread out and hilly, so walking works within a neighbourhood rather than between them. Taxis are metered, plentiful and cheap by European standards. The high-speed train to Istanbul takes about four and a half hours and to Konya under two, both from Ankara YHT station, and is much more pleasant than flying. Esenboga airport is 28km north with a frequent Havas bus. Traffic is heavy at rush hour and driving is not recommended for newcomers.
ankara.visas: Turkey grants most Western passports a 90-day stay in any 180-day period, with EU, UK and Canadian citizens entering visa-free and some nationalities needing an e-Visa bought online in advance. Turkey has no digital nomad visa in the usual sense, but it does have a short-term residence permit, the kisa donem ikamet, which is the standard route for anyone staying longer. It is applied for online through the e-ikamet system, requires proof of address, health insurance and funds, and has become noticeably harder to obtain in Istanbul in recent years. Ankara is generally reported as more straightforward. Turkey also has a well-known citizenship-by-investment property route. Anyone planning to stay should start the residence process well before the 90 days expire.
ankara.bestTime: Ankara sits on the Anatolian plateau at about 900 metres, which gives it a genuinely continental climate and four distinct seasons. Spring, April to early June, and autumn, September to October, are the best: warm days, cool nights, clear light and comfortable walking weather. Summer is hot and very dry, with highs in the low thirties, but the altitude keeps nights cool and the humidity is low, so it is far more bearable than the coast. Winter, December to February, is genuinely cold, regularly below freezing, with snow and grey skies, and air quality dips as heating ramps up. There is no tourist season to speak of, so accommodation prices are stable year-round, which is one quiet advantage of a city that does not live on visitors.
ankara.prosCons: Ankara is cheap, functional and largely undiscovered by remote workers, which is either its main appeal or its main problem depending on what you want. It has a real metro, excellent and inexpensive food, a serious university and technology sector, fast internet, and a central position that puts the whole of Anatolia within reach by good trains. It is far calmer and less crowded than Istanbul. Against that, it is not a beautiful city, the tourist sights amount to a strong museum and a hilltop citadel, and there is almost no international nomad community. English is limited outside the universities and technology parks. Winters are cold and the air quality suffers. Anyone arriving expecting Istanbul's drama will find a working capital instead.
ankara.whoFor: Ankara suits remote workers who want to live in Turkey properly rather than pass through it, who are willing to learn some Turkish, and who value low costs and a functioning city over scenery and company. It works well for anyone building ties to the Turkish technology sector, for people who want a base for exploring Anatolia by train, and for those who find Istanbul overwhelming or too expensive. It is a reasonable choice for families, with safe neighbourhoods and good private schools. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs an English-speaking environment, an existing nomad crowd, beach access or nightlife on any scale. Those wanting Turkey with all of that should look at Istanbul, Izmir or the coast.

olomouc.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Olomouc, which buys a standard of central European city living that would cost half as much again in Prague. A one-bedroom apartment in or near the historic centre runs about $450 to $600, and the panel-block districts a tram ride out drop that to $350 to $450. Groceries land around $220 to $280. A pub lunch with a beer is $7 to $9, a good restaurant dinner $18 to $25, and Czech beer remains cheaper than soft drinks at about $1.60 for half a litre. A monthly transit pass is roughly $18. Utilities add $90 to $150 and rise in winter. The city's student population keeps prices honest in a way that tourist-heavy Czech towns do not manage.
olomouc.whereToWork: Olomouc has a small but real coworking scene, mostly serving the university and a growing cluster of software companies, with desks at roughly $90 to $140 a month. The bigger asset is Palacky University, the second oldest in the country, whose 20,000 students support a dense network of cafes that are entirely comfortable with laptops and long stays. The lanes around Horni namesti and Univerzitni street have most of them. Czech fixed-line internet is fast and cheap, and mobile data is reliable if not especially generous. Because the city is compact, you can reasonably keep two or three regular working spots within a ten-minute walk of home, which is a practical advantage over larger cities where changing scene costs half an hour.
olomouc.gettingAround: Olomouc is a walking city first: the historic centre is about a kilometre across and closed to most traffic, and almost everything a resident needs sits inside or just beyond it. Beyond that, an efficient tram network with several lines covers the wider city, running from early morning to around eleven at night, with a monthly pass at about $18 and single tickets under a dollar. Cycling is popular and the terrain is flat. The main railway station is a fifteen-minute tram ride from the centre and puts Prague at two hours and twenty minutes, Brno at an hour, and Vienna, Krakow and Bratislava all within half a day. There is no airport; most people fly into Prague, Brno, Vienna or Katowice and take a train.
olomouc.visas: The Czech Republic is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so EU and EEA citizens may live and work here without formality beyond registering after 30 days. Most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180-day Schengen period. Since 2023 the Czech Republic has operated a digital nomad visa, aimed at highly skilled non-EU remote workers from a defined list of countries, which grants a long-stay permit of up to one year and is one of the more usable schemes in central Europe. Outside that, the long-standing zivnostensky list, the Czech trade licence, remains the route many freelancers use, though it involves real bureaucracy and is best approached with a local accountant. Applications are made at Czech consulates abroad rather than in-country.
olomouc.bestTime: May to September is the clear window. Late spring brings long light evenings, the university in full session and the squares busy, while June to August is warm without the heat that makes southern Europe uncomfortable, with highs in the mid to high twenties. September is arguably the best month of all: warm days, thinner crowds, and the new academic year filling the cafes again. Autumn turns grey and wet through October and November. Winter, December to February, is cold, often below freezing, with short days and occasional snow that suits the baroque centre very well; the Christmas market on Horni namesti is one of the better ones in the country and far less crowded than Prague's. March and April are unreliable and best avoided.
olomouc.prosCons: Olomouc offers a UNESCO-listed baroque centre, a serious university, Czech prices well below Prague and a genuinely walkable scale, which together make it one of central Europe's better-value bases. Beer is cheap and excellent, trains connect it to half the region, the streets are safe, and the student population keeps the city young without making it loud. Against that, it is small. The international community is thin, the nomad scene barely exists, and English, while common among students, is not universal. There is no airport and winters are long, grey and cold. Anyone wanting mountains, sea or a large city's variety will find Olomouc limiting, and those needing frequent international flights will spend a lot of time on trains to Prague or Vienna.
olomouc.whoFor: Olomouc suits remote workers who want central European quality of life at a price that leaves room to save, and who are happy to supply their own social life or draw it from a university town. It is a strong choice for anyone using the Czech digital nomad visa or trade licence, for people who want to be within a few hours of Prague, Vienna, Krakow and Brno without paying capital-city rent, and for cyclists and beer drinkers. It works well for couples and for quiet, focused work. It suits less well anyone who needs an established nomad crowd, warm weather, an airport at hand or a large English-speaking professional network. Brno is the obvious step up in size while keeping most of the price advantage.

pecs.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $850 a month as a solo remote worker in Pécs, which is among the cheaper options anywhere in the European Union. A one-bedroom apartment in the centre runs about $300 to $420, and the surrounding districts drop that to $230 to $320. Groceries land around $180 to $240, with the Saturday market on Vasarcsarnok cheaper than the supermarkets for produce. A menu lunch is $5 to $7, a restaurant dinner with wine $15 to $22, and Hungarian wine from the nearby Villany region is very good and very cheap. A monthly transit pass is about $16. Utilities add $80 to $150, more in winter. The university keeps a large stock of small flats in circulation, which holds rents down outside the September rush.
pecs.whereToWork: Pécs is a university city of roughly 20,000 students, and the working infrastructure follows from that rather than from any nomad economy. There are one or two small coworking spaces attached to the university's innovation ecosystem, with desks around $80 to $130 a month, but most people work from home or from cafes. The pedestrianised Kiraly utca and the streets around Szechenyi ter have a good density of places that will not hurry you along. Hungarian fixed-line internet is fast and cheap, among the better networks in the region, and mobile data is inexpensive. The main practical constraint is that very little of this is set up for foreigners: expect Hungarian menus, Hungarian signage and a certain amount of translation-app work in the first weeks.
pecs.gettingAround: Pécs is compact and hilly, built on the southern slope of the Mecsek, and the centre is comfortably walkable if you accept some climbing. A bus network covers the rest of the city, with a monthly pass at about $16 and single tickets under a dollar; there are no trams. Cycling works on the flat but is hard work towards the hills. The railway station is a fifteen-minute walk from the centre and connects to Budapest in about three hours, which is the main link most residents use. There is no useful airport: Budapest is the practical gateway, roughly three hours away by train or car. Within the region a car opens up the Villany wine country and the Danube, but nothing essential requires one.
pecs.visas: Hungary is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so EU and EEA citizens face no restrictions beyond registering a residence address. Most other Western passports receive 90 days in any 180-day Schengen period. Hungary operated a well-publicised White Card digital nomad residence permit, introduced in 2022 for non-EU remote workers earning above a set threshold from foreign sources, and it remains one of the few purpose-built schemes in the region; requirements and thresholds have been revised since launch, so check the current figures with a Hungarian consulate rather than relying on older summaries. Beyond that the usual routes are employment, study at the university, which has English-language medical and business programmes, or family reunification. Bureaucracy is real and generally conducted in Hungarian.
pecs.bestTime: Pécs enjoys a mild, almost Mediterranean pocket of climate by Hungarian standards, sheltered by the Mecsek hills, and it shows. May, June and September are the best months: warm, bright and comfortable, with the squares full and the surrounding wine country at its most pleasant. July and August get hot, into the low to mid thirties, though it is a dry heat and evenings on the terraces are the point of the season. Autumn is long and golden through October, and the Villany harvest festivals fall in this window. Winter, December to February, is cold, grey and damp rather than snowy, and the city is quiet with students away over Christmas. March and April are changeable. The academic year fills the city from late September.
pecs.prosCons: Pécs offers genuine European Union living at close to south-east Asian prices, with a two-thousand-year history that runs from Roman tombs through a surviving Ottoman mosque to a well-preserved Habsburg centre. It is warm by Hungarian standards, safe, walkable, and surrounded by good wine country. The university gives it energy and a supply of cheap flats. Against that, it is isolated: Budapest is three hours away and there is no airport. The international community is very small and the nomad scene effectively nonexistent. English is limited outside the university, and Hungarian is a difficult language with no useful cognates. Winter is long and grey. Anyone needing a professional network, frequent flights or an English-speaking environment will struggle here.
pecs.whoFor: Pécs suits remote workers who want to spend very little, live somewhere genuinely old and attractive, and do not need company to be provided for them. It works well for people on the Hungarian White Card, for anyone studying at the university's English-language programmes, for writers and researchers who want quiet, and for wine drinkers with a car. Couples and solo workers who are comfortable in their own company will get the most from it. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs an existing foreign community, easy international travel, or a city where daily life can be conducted in English. Budapest is the obvious alternative for those who want Hungary with all of that, at roughly double the rent.

rijeka.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Rijeka, which makes it markedly cheaper than Split or Dubrovnik for a city with better year-round infrastructure. A one-bedroom apartment near the centre runs about $500 to $700, and the hillside districts above the port drop that to $400 to $550. Because Rijeka is a working city rather than a resort, long leases are available on normal terms and do not vanish in summer, which is a real advantage over the Dalmatian coast. Groceries land around $250 to $320. A konoba lunch is $10 to $14, a restaurant dinner $22 to $32, and coffee about $2. A monthly transit pass is roughly $30. Utilities add $110 to $190, higher in the damp winter months.
rijeka.whereToWork: Rijeka has a modest coworking scene, with a few spaces in and around the centre charging roughly $110 to $180 a month, and the city's designation as European Capital of Culture in 2020 left behind some renovated cultural venues that double as working space. The Korzo, the main pedestrian street, and the streets running off it have plenty of cafes where a laptop is unremarkable, and Croatian coffee culture is famously unhurried, so nobody will move you along. Fixed-line internet is fast and mobile data is good and cheap within the EU roaming area. The practical advantage over the tourist coast is that all of this works in February as well as in August, when Split's cafes are full of visitors and its rents have tripled.
rijeka.gettingAround: Rijeka is built on a narrow shelf between the Kvarner gulf and the hills, which makes it long, thin and steep. The centre is walkable end to end along the waterfront and the Korzo, but anything uphill is a serious climb and the city has stairs where other places have streets. An extensive bus network covers the rest, with a monthly pass at about $30. The main railway station connects to Zagreb in around four hours, which is slower than the bus at two and a half. Rijeka airport is on the island of Krk, 30km away, seasonal and small; Zagreb, Pula, Trieste and Ljubljana are all realistic alternatives within a few hours. Ferries run along the coast and to the Kvarner islands in season.
rijeka.visas: Croatia is in the European Union, the Schengen area since January 2023, and the eurozone since the same date, so EU and EEA citizens may live and work here freely. Most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180-day Schengen period. Croatia was an early mover on remote work and its digital nomad residence permit, available since 2021, grants up to one year for non-EU nationals working for foreign employers, with an income threshold and proof of accommodation and health insurance required. It is not renewable directly, requiring a gap before reapplying. Notably, income earned under it is not subject to Croatian income tax, which is unusual among such schemes and one reason the permit has been popular.
rijeka.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months in Rijeka: warm, bright and free of the July and August crowds that fill the Kvarner coast. Summer is hot, into the low thirties, and the city empties towards the islands and beaches at Opatija and Lovran along the coast. Winter is mild by continental standards, around 10 degrees, but wet, and Rijeka is known for the bura, a fierce dry wind off the mountains that can blow for days and closes the coastal road. February brings the Rijeka Carnival, one of the largest in Europe and the single most distinctive thing in the local calendar. Because the city works year-round rather than seasonally, rents and services stay stable in a way the Dalmatian resorts do not manage.
rijeka.prosCons: Rijeka gives you the Croatian coast without the resort economy: real neighbourhoods, year-round rents, a working port, a university, and a cultural scene that outlasted its Capital of Culture year. It is cheaper than Split, better connected to central Europe, and has the Kvarner islands and the Ucka mountains within half an hour. The digital nomad permit is one of the better ones in the EU. Against that, it is not conventionally pretty: the centre is handsome Habsburg but the surroundings are industrial and socialist-era. The bura wind is genuinely unpleasant. Beaches are pebbly and mostly a bus ride away. The nomad community is small, with most of Croatia's remote workers in Split, Zagreb or Zadar, and winters are wet.
rijeka.whoFor: Rijeka suits remote workers who want to live on the Adriatic year-round rather than visit it in summer, and who would rather have a functioning city than a postcard. It is a strong choice for anyone on Croatia's digital nomad permit who wants stable rent, for people who value proximity to Slovenia, Italy and Austria, and for those who sail, hike or want island access without resort prices. It works for couples and solo workers who make their own social plans. It suits less well anyone chasing a large nomad scene, guaranteed sunshine, sandy beaches or the picture-postcard Dalmatia of Split and Dubrovnik, all of which are a few hours south and considerably more expensive.

ioannina.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,050 a month as a solo remote worker in Ioannina, which is cheap for Greece and very cheap for a lakeside university city in the European Union. A one-bedroom apartment near the centre or the castle quarter runs about $350 to $500, and the student districts drop that to $280 to $400. Rents rise noticeably in September when the university intake arrives, so arriving in summer and signing early is worth doing. Groceries land around $220 to $280. A souvlaki lunch is $4 to $6, a taverna dinner with wine $15 to $22, and coffee, which in Greece is a two-hour institution rather than a drink, about $3.50. Utilities add $90 to $180, higher in the cold Epirus winter.
ioannina.whereToWork: Ioannina's working infrastructure comes from the University of Ioannina and its 20,000 students rather than from any remote-work economy. There is a small coworking presence connected to the university's research and innovation activity, with desks in the region of $90 to $140 a month, but most people use cafes. The lakeside promenade and the streets inside the old castle walls have a dense supply of them, and Greek cafe culture actively expects you to occupy a table for hours over one frappe. Fixed-line internet is decent and improving, mobile data is cheap and reliable across the EU roaming area. The practical limitation is that almost nothing here is designed with foreign remote workers in mind, so expect Greek as the working language outside the university.
ioannina.gettingAround: Ioannina is compact and flat around the lake, and the centre, the castle quarter and the lakefront are all comfortably walkable. A city bus network covers the outer districts and the university campus, with single tickets around $1.30. Most residents walk or cycle. The lake itself is the defining feature: a small ferry runs to the island of Nisi, where a cluster of monasteries and the house where Ali Pasha was killed sit among the reeds. Long-distance buses from the KTEL station connect to Athens in about five and a half hours and Thessaloniki in four, both on the excellent Egnatia motorway. Ioannina has a small airport with domestic flights to Athens. A car is the practical way into the Zagori villages and the Vikos gorge.
ioannina.visas: Greece is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so EU and EEA citizens may live and work here with no formality beyond registering for a tax number and social security if they work locally. Most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180-day Schengen period. Greece introduced a digital nomad visa in 2021 for non-EU remote workers, requiring a minimum monthly income from foreign sources, health insurance and a clean record; it grants a year initially and can convert into a two-year residence permit. Greece also offers a 50 percent income tax exemption for seven years to qualifying new tax residents who relocate and commit to staying, which has drawn a fair number of returning Greeks and some foreigners.
ioannina.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months. Ioannina sits at 480 metres in the Epirus mountains, which makes its summers hotter and drier than the coast but its evenings genuinely cool, and the lake moderates the worst of it. July and August reach the mid thirties and the city empties as Greeks head for the sea. Autumn is long and beautiful, with the Pindus turning colour through October and November. Winter is the real surprise: Ioannina is one of the wettest and coldest cities in Greece, with snow, frequent rain and temperatures near freezing, and the nearby Zagori villages become a proper ski and mountain destination. The university term from October to May keeps the city awake through it.
ioannina.prosCons: Ioannina is one of the few Greek cities that is neither an island resort nor Athens, and that is its appeal: a real, working, lakeside university town with an Ottoman castle quarter, silversmithing traditions, and the Vikos gorge and Zagori villages an hour away. It is cheap, safe, walkable and green, and the food is excellent. Against that, it is remote by Greek standards, five hours from Athens, and its airport is tiny. There is no international community to speak of and no nomad scene at all. Winters are genuinely cold and wet, which is not what most people picture when they think of Greece. English is common among students and much less so elsewhere, and the summer heat is real.
ioannina.whoFor: Ioannina suits remote workers who want Greece without the islands: mountains, a lake, a university town, and prices that leave room to save. It is a strong choice for hikers and climbers, given the Vikos gorge and the Pindus range on the doorstep, and for anyone on the Greek digital nomad visa who wants to spend less than Athens or Thessaloniki would cost. It works well for solo workers and couples who make their own plans. It is a poor fit for anyone expecting beaches, guaranteed sun, an existing foreign community or easy international flights. Thessaloniki, four hours away, is the obvious step up for those who want a bigger city while staying in northern Greece.

naxos.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,400 a month as a solo remote worker on Naxos, which sits comfortably below Mykonos and Santorini while offering more actual island. A one-bedroom apartment in Chora runs about $500 to $750 on a long winter lease, but this is the central financial fact of island life: summer short-lets earn owners far more, so year-round contracts are scarce and best negotiated from October. Village rentals inland are cheaper. Groceries land around $280 to $360, with a premium on anything shipped in and a discount on what the island grows, which on Naxos is a great deal: potatoes, cheese, citrus and meat. A taverna dinner is $18 to $28, coffee $3.50, and the ferry to Athens $40 to $70.
naxos.whereToWork: Naxos has no coworking space in the sense a city dweller would recognise, and anyone coming here works from their accommodation or from cafes. Chora has a reasonable supply of the latter along the waterfront and up in the Bourgos, and they are relaxed about long stays outside the August crush. The practical issue is connectivity: fixed-line speeds in Chora are adequate and in the inland villages can be poor, so checking the actual connection before signing anything is essential rather than cautious. Mobile 4G coverage is good across most of the island and many residents keep a data plan as a fallback for calls. Greek EU roaming makes that cheap. Power cuts are occasional but not rare in winter storms.
naxos.gettingAround: Chora is walkable and largely pedestrian in its old quarter, a maze of whitewashed lanes climbing to the Venetian kastro. Beyond it, Naxos is the largest of the Cyclades and you need transport: a bus network links Chora to the main beaches and the larger inland villages such as Filoti and Apiranthos, running frequently in summer and sparsely in winter. Most residents rent a scooter, a quad or a small car, and a car is close to essential from November to March. The port is the island's link to everything: fast ferries reach Athens in three and a half hours and conventional ones in five, with connections across the Cyclades. There is a small airport with flights to Athens, mostly seasonal.
naxos.visas: Greece is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so EU and EEA citizens may live and work on Naxos without restriction. Most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180-day Schengen period, which is the constraint that shapes most non-EU stays here. The Greek digital nomad visa, introduced in 2021, is the usual longer route: it requires a minimum monthly income earned from outside Greece, health insurance and a clean record, grants a year and can convert to a two-year residence permit. Greece's 50 percent income tax break for qualifying new tax residents applies here as anywhere in the country. Island bureaucracy is slower than Athens and generally conducted in Greek, so a local accountant is worth the fee.
naxos.bestTime: May, June, September and early October are the best months on Naxos: warm sea, long days, open tavernas and none of the August pressure. July and August are hot, busy and expensive, and the meltemi wind blows hard through them, which windsurfers at Mikri Vigla consider the whole point and everyone else finds tiring. What sets Naxos apart from its neighbours is that it does not close: it has a real agricultural economy and a resident population of around 18,000, so unlike Santorini or Ios there are open shops, a working school and a functioning town through the winter. Winter is mild, around 15 degrees, wet and windy, with ferries occasionally cancelled for days at a time.
naxos.prosCons: Naxos is the Cyclades island that works year-round: big enough to have mountains, farms and a dozen villages, cheap enough to live on, and populated enough not to shut in October. The beaches on the west coast run for kilometres and are rarely full, the food is the best in the island group because the island grows it, and Chora is genuinely beautiful without being a film set. Against that, it is an island: ferries are the lifeline and weather cancels them, medical care beyond a health centre means flying to Athens, and internet quality varies sharply by address. Year-round rentals are hard to find and summer prices are punishing. There is no nomad community and winter is quiet to the point of isolation.
naxos.whoFor: Naxos suits remote workers who genuinely want island life rather than an island holiday, and who have the discipline to work without an office or a community to structure their week. It rewards swimmers, hikers, windsurfers and cooks. It is a good choice for couples, for anyone on the Greek digital nomad visa looking for somewhere cheaper and more real than Santorini, and for people who plan to stay long enough to find a proper year-round lease. It suits less well anyone who needs reliable high-speed internet as a non-negotiable, frequent international travel, a professional network, or company in February. Athens is three and a half hours away by fast ferry and answers all of those.

alanya.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $950 a month as a solo remote worker in Alanya, which buys a Mediterranean seafront life at a fraction of the Spanish or Italian equivalent. A one-bedroom apartment a few streets back from the beach runs about $300 to $450 on a long lease, with sea-view and newer complexes reaching $600 or more. Alanya has a large foreign resident population and a correspondingly organised rental market, much of it conducted in English, Russian and German. Groceries land around $200 to $260, with the weekly pazar market far cheaper than supermarkets. A lokanta lunch is $4 to $6, a restaurant dinner with drinks $15 to $25, and a monthly transit pass about $20. Utilities add $60 to $130, with summer air conditioning the main variable.
alanya.whereToWork: Alanya's working infrastructure is built around its resident foreign population rather than around a nomad scene. There are a couple of small coworking spaces and a number of cafes, particularly in the Oba and Cikcilli districts where many foreign residents live, that are entirely used to laptops. Rates where coworking exists run about $80 to $140 a month. Turkish fixed-line internet is fast and inexpensive, and this is a well-connected town rather than a remote resort. The one recurring problem for foreigners is Turkey's handset registration rule: a foreign phone stops working on Turkish networks after 120 days unless registered and taxed, which is expensive, so most long-stayers buy a cheap local handset or plan around it.
alanya.gettingAround: Alanya is strung out along the coast, with the castle headland at the centre and residential districts running several kilometres either side, so walking works within a district and not between them. Dolmus minibuses run constantly along the coastal road, cost under a dollar and are the way almost everyone moves; they stop wherever you flag them. Taxis are metered and cheap. Many foreign residents keep a scooter or a small car, which is genuinely useful for the Taurus mountains behind the town. Antalya airport is about two hours west by bus, and the newer Gazipasa airport is 40 minutes east with a growing list of European routes. Long-distance buses from the otogar reach most of Turkey overnight and comfortably.
alanya.visas: Turkey grants most Western passports 90 days in any 180, with EU, UK and Canadian citizens entering visa-free. There is no digital nomad visa as such. The standard route for longer stays is the short-term residence permit, the kisa donem ikamet, applied for online through the e-ikamet system with proof of address, health insurance and funds. Alanya has a very large foreign resident community and a corresponding industry of agents who handle these applications, which makes the process considerably less painful here than doing it alone. Note that Turkey has restricted new residence permit registrations in some neighbourhoods where the foreign population exceeds a threshold, and Alanya has been affected, so check the current status of a specific address before signing a lease.
alanya.bestTime: April, May, September and October are the best months in Alanya: sea warm enough to swim, air in the mid twenties, and the resort machinery running without the July crush. Summer is hot and humid, regularly into the mid thirties with high humidity off the sea, and the town fills with package holidaymakers. Winter is the quiet secret: mild at 15 to 18 degrees in the day, sunny more often than not, cheap, and with a substantial population of northern Europeans who overwinter here precisely for that. Some restaurants and hotels close from November to March but far from all, because the resident foreign community keeps enough of the town open. The sea is swimmable from roughly May to November.
alanya.prosCons: Alanya offers a genuinely warm Mediterranean coast, a long swimming season, low prices and an established international community, which makes the practical business of settling in far easier than in most Turkish towns. Healthcare is good and cheap, food is excellent, the Taurus mountains are twenty minutes inland, and Gazipasa airport is close. Against that, it is a resort, and in summer it behaves like one: crowded, loud in places, and oriented towards package tourism. Much of the architecture is undistinguished concrete. The foreign community is more retiree and property-buyer than remote worker, so the nomad scene is thin. Turkish inflation makes budgeting in lira unpredictable, residence permit rules have tightened, and summer humidity is genuinely uncomfortable.
alanya.whoFor: Alanya suits remote workers who want warm sea, low costs and an easy landing, and who do not need a nomad community to be waiting for them. It works well for people who plan to overwinter somewhere sunny, for anyone with family in tow who values an established foreign infrastructure of schools, doctors and English-speaking agents, and for water sports and hiking. It is a reasonable base for exploring the Turkish coast and Cappadocia. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting a young remote-work scene, an unspoilt town, or a city's cultural depth. Antalya an hour and a half west is larger and more varied, and Izmir is the better choice for anyone who wants a real Turkish city on the sea.

constanta.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $900 a month as a solo remote worker in Constanța, which makes Romania's Black Sea port one of the cheapest coastal cities in the European Union. A one-bedroom apartment in the centre or the Faleza Nord district runs about $300 to $450, and the older blocks further out drop to $220 to $320. Rents rise sharply in the summer season along the beach strip at Mamaia, which is effectively a separate resort economy, so living in the city proper rather than the resort saves a great deal. Groceries land around $200 to $260. A lunch is $5 to $8, a restaurant dinner with wine $15 to $22, and a monthly transit pass about $12. Utilities add $80 to $160, higher in winter.
constanta.whereToWork: Constanța has a modest coworking scene, with a handful of spaces in the centre charging roughly $80 to $130 a month, serving local software and logistics firms rather than visiting nomads. Romania's real advantage is infrastructure: fixed-line internet here is among the fastest and cheapest anywhere in Europe, gigabit connections are routine and inexpensive, and mobile data is excellent. That single fact makes working from an apartment entirely practical. Cafes in the old town near the Casino and along Stefan cel Mare are comfortable with laptops. English is reasonably common among younger people and in the technology sector, less so elsewhere. The summer influx to Mamaia changes the atmosphere of the whole city from June to September.
constanta.gettingAround: Constanța is spread along the coast and the centre is walkable, particularly the peninsula around the old town, the Casino and the port. Buses and trolleybuses cover the rest of the city cheaply, with a monthly pass around $12. Mamaia, the resort strip north of the city, is a short bus ride and connected by a summer cable car. Bucharest is about two and a half hours by car on the A2 motorway and three to four by train, which is the main link most residents use; the capital's Otopeni airport is the practical international gateway. Constanța has its own small airport with limited seasonal routes. The Danube Delta, one of Europe's great wetlands, is around two hours north.
constanta.visas: Romania is in the European Union and joined the Schengen area for air and sea borders in March 2024, with full land border accession following in January 2025, so Schengen rules now apply. EU and EEA citizens may live and work freely. Most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180. Romania introduced a digital nomad visa in 2021 for non-EU remote workers, requiring proof of foreign income at a multiple of the Romanian average wage, health insurance and a clean record; it grants an initial stay that can be extended. Romania is also well known for its low corporate tax rates for micro-companies and its flat personal income tax, which has attracted a meaningful number of foreign founders to register here.
constanta.bestTime: May, June and September are the best months in Constanța. The Black Sea is swimmable from roughly June to September, and July and August bring the full Romanian holiday season to Mamaia, which triples the population of the strip and fills the restaurants. September is the sweet spot: warm sea, thinning crowds and prices dropping back. Spring is pleasant and windy. Winter is cold, grey and windy off the sea, with temperatures around freezing and a city that feels considerably larger than its off-season population, since much of the coastal infrastructure shuts entirely from October to April. Anyone planning to stay year-round should base themselves in the city rather than in the resort, where winter can be genuinely desolate.
constanta.prosCons: Constanța gives you EU residency, a Black Sea coast, Roman and Greek archaeology going back two and a half thousand years, and some of the fastest cheap internet in Europe, all at prices well under the Mediterranean. The old town around the Casino is handsome, the Danube Delta is close, and Bucharest is a comfortable drive. Against that, the city has real neglect: parts of the historic quarter are derelict, and investment has gone to the resort rather than to the centre. The Black Sea is not the Mediterranean, with a short swimming season and a cold, bleak winter. There is essentially no nomad community, English is patchy, and Mamaia's summer club economy dominates the season whether you want it or not.
constanta.whoFor: Constanța suits remote workers who want a European Union base with a coastline and very low costs, and who value fast internet and Romania's tax arrangements over scenery. It works well for anyone on the Romanian digital nomad visa or running a micro-company, for people interested in the classical archaeology of the region, and for those who want the Danube Delta within reach. It is a reasonable summer base and a demanding winter one. It is a poor fit for anyone expecting Mediterranean warmth, an established foreign community, or a well-maintained historic city. Bucharest, two and a half hours away, has the jobs, the flights and the scene; Constanța has the sea and the quiet.

iasi.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $850 a month as a solo remote worker in Iași, which is remarkable value for a European Union city with a large software sector and 60,000 students. A one-bedroom apartment in Copou, Tudor Vladimirescu or near the centre runs about $300 to $420, with newer developments in Palas and Miroslava reaching $450 to $600. Groceries land around $190 to $250. A business lunch is $6 to $9, a restaurant dinner with wine $15 to $22, and Moldavian wine from the surrounding hills is very cheap and rather good. A monthly transit pass is about $12. Utilities add $80 to $160, more in the cold winter. Student demand tightens the market sharply each September, so timing a lease matters.
iasi.whereToWork: Iași is one of Romania's principal technology cities, with a large outsourcing and product-development sector built around its universities, and the working infrastructure reflects that properly. There are several coworking spaces at roughly $90 to $150 a month, plus the technology parks that host companies like Amazon, Oracle and a long list of local firms. Fixed-line internet is exceptional: gigabit fibre is normal and costs a fraction of western European prices, which is one of Romania's genuine competitive advantages. Cafes around Copou and the pedestrianised centre are used to laptops. English is widely spoken among the technology and student populations, considerably more so than in most Romanian cities of this size, which makes settling in easier.
iasi.gettingAround: Iași is hilly and spread across seven hills, with a walkable centre running from Palas and the Palace of Culture up Stefan cel Mare to Piata Unirii and on to the university district at Copou. Trams and buses cover the rest, cheaply, with a monthly pass around $12; the tram network is old but extensive. Most residents walk in the centre and use transit or a taxi beyond it, with ride-hailing apps widely used and inexpensive. Iași international airport has grown substantially and now flies to a good spread of European cities, which is a real advantage over comparable Romanian cities. Bucharest is about six hours by train or an hour by air; Chisinau in Moldova is around three hours by road.
iasi.visas: Romania is in the European Union and completed Schengen accession for land borders in January 2025, so Schengen rules apply. EU and EEA citizens may live and work without restriction. Most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180. Romania's digital nomad visa, in place since 2021, is available to non-EU remote workers who can show foreign-sourced income at a multiple of the Romanian average wage, along with health insurance and a clean criminal record. Romania is also attractive for company formation: the micro-company regime and flat personal income tax rates are low by EU standards, and Iași's large accounting and legal sector is used to handling foreign founders. Registration procedures are conducted in Romanian and an agent is worth the cost.
iasi.bestTime: May, June and September are the best months in Iași: warm, bright and with the city at its most active. Summer, July and August, is hot, into the low thirties, and the student population disappears, which makes the city noticeably quieter and the rental market briefly loose. Autumn is long and attractive through October, and the wine harvest in the surrounding Moldavian hills falls in this window. Winter is genuinely cold, regularly below freezing with snow from December to February, and the hills make icy pavements a real consideration. The academic year from October brings the city fully to life. Iași's patron saint festival in mid-October draws enormous pilgrim crowds and fills every hotel, which is worth knowing about in advance.
iasi.prosCons: Iași combines a serious technology sector, very low costs, fast cheap internet and a growing airport, which is an unusually practical combination. It has real cultural weight as the historic capital of Moldavia, with the Palace of Culture, a strong university tradition and the best-preserved literary heritage in Romania. English is common in the professional and student population. Against that, the city is far from the rest of Europe by land, six hours from Bucharest, and its position near the Moldovan and Ukrainian borders has felt less peripheral since 2022. Winters are hard. The nomad community is essentially nonexistent, as foreign arrivals here are usually employed by local technology firms rather than passing through.
iasi.whoFor: Iași suits remote workers who want European Union living at close to the cheapest price it comes, with genuinely good infrastructure and a professional environment where English works. It is a strong choice for software people who want colleagues rather than tourists, for anyone using Romania's digital nomad visa or micro-company regime, and for those who value a real city with universities and history over scenery. It works for solo workers and families alike, with good private schooling and safe neighbourhoods. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting warmth, a coast, an existing nomad scene, or short flights to western Europe. Cluj-Napoca is the better-known Romanian technology city and Bucharest the better-connected one, both at higher cost.

vlore.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $750 a month as a solo remote worker in Vlorë, which makes it one of the cheapest coastal cities in Europe. A one-bedroom apartment near the seafront runs about $250 to $400 on a long lease, with newer builds along the Lungomare promenade at the upper end and older blocks inland at the lower. Summer short-lets are far more expensive, so a year-round contract signed in autumn is the sensible approach. Groceries land around $170 to $230, with local produce very cheap and imported goods less so. A meal in a local restaurant is $6 to $10, a seafood dinner with wine $15 to $22, and coffee about $1. A monthly transit pass is negligible; most people walk. Utilities add $50 to $110.
vlore.whereToWork: Vlorë has no established coworking scene, and remote workers here work from apartments or cafes. Albanian cafe culture is dense and unhurried, and the seafront promenade has a long line of places where a laptop draws no attention. The practical constraint is connectivity: Albania's fixed-line internet has improved considerably and fibre is available in the newer buildings along the seafront, but older stock can be poor, so testing the actual connection before signing is essential. Mobile data is cheap and 4G coverage along the coast is good, which makes tethering a workable backup. Tirana, two hours away, has the country's coworking spaces and technology community if you need them occasionally. English is common among younger Albanians.
vlore.gettingAround: Vlorë is walkable along its seafront, and the Lungomare promenade, rebuilt in recent years, runs for several kilometres and functions as the city's main artery for walking and cycling. Furgon minibuses and city buses cover the rest cheaply. Most residents walk. The city is the gateway to the Albanian Riviera: the Llogara pass climbs south into the mountains and drops down to Himarë, Dhërmi and Sarandë, and a car or scooter transforms what is reachable. Buses run south along that road in summer and less often in winter. Tirana is about two hours north by the SH8 and the motorway, and Tirana airport is the country's only significant international gateway. Ferries cross to Brindisi in Italy from the port.
vlore.visas: Albania is not in the European Union or Schengen, and it has one of the most generous entry policies in Europe: most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, receive 90 days visa-free, and US citizens are granted a full year. That single fact makes Albania unusually easy for non-EU remote workers who have exhausted their Schengen allowance. Albania introduced a Unique Permit that covers residence and work in one application, and has publicised a digital nomad arrangement for remote workers, though the practical experience of applying is still developing and the rules have shifted since launch. Anyone planning to stay beyond the visa-free period should confirm the current position with an Albanian consulate or a local lawyer.
vlore.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months in Vlorë: warm sea, comfortable air in the mid twenties, and the coast open but not overrun. July and August are hot, into the low thirties, and the Albanian Riviera fills with domestic and regional holidaymakers, pushing prices up sharply and the beaches to capacity. Winter is mild, around 12 to 15 degrees in the day, wet, and very quiet, with much of the coastal tourism infrastructure closed from November to April. Vlorë itself, unlike the smaller Riviera villages, is a real city of over 100,000 and stays open through the winter, which makes it a far more practical year-round base than Himarë or Ksamil.
vlore.prosCons: Vlorë sits where the Adriatic meets the Ionian, which is a genuinely dramatic piece of geography, and it offers a warm coast at prices no European Union country can match. Albania's visa-free allowance is the longest in the region, the food is good and cheap, the people are notably welcoming to foreigners, and the Riviera south of the Llogara pass is one of the last stretches of undeveloped Mediterranean coast. Against that, infrastructure is uneven: roads, water supply and internet all vary by address. Construction is everywhere and often unattractive. There is no nomad community and very little English outside the young. Healthcare beyond basics means Tirana, and the beaches in the city itself are unremarkable compared with those further south.
vlore.whoFor: Vlorë suits remote workers who want a warm coast on a very small budget, who have used up their Schengen days and need somewhere in Europe that does not count against them, and who are comfortable with a country that is still visibly building itself. It works well for people who want a real city rather than a resort as a base for exploring the Albanian Riviera, and for anyone who values low cost and long visa-free stays above polish. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs reliable infrastructure as a given, an English-speaking environment, an established foreign community or good healthcare nearby. Tirana is the practical alternative for those wanting Albania with more of all of that.

hercegnovi.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,150 a month as a solo remote worker in Herceg Novi, which is cheaper than Kotor or Budva for a comparable position on the Bay of Kotor. A one-bedroom apartment on the slopes above the old town runs about $400 to $600 on a long lease, with sea views adding a premium and the flat land near Igalo costing slightly less. Summer short-lets are far more lucrative for owners, so year-round contracts are best negotiated from October onwards. Groceries land around $260 to $330. A konoba meal is $10 to $16, a seafood dinner with wine $22 to $32, and coffee about $2. Montenegro uses the euro despite not being in the eurozone, which keeps prices legible.
hercegnovi.whereToWork: Herceg Novi has no significant coworking scene; the country's small remote-work infrastructure sits mostly in Podgorica, Kotor and Budva. People here work from apartments and from cafes along the Šetalište Pet Danica promenade, where sitting for hours over a coffee is entirely normal. Fixed-line internet in the town is generally adequate and fibre is available in newer buildings, but the older stone housing on the hillside can be poorly served, so testing the connection before committing to a lease is worth the trouble. Mobile 4G is good along the coast. Montenegro is not in the EU, so EU roaming does not apply and a local SIM is the sensible purchase on arrival.
hercegnovi.gettingAround: Herceg Novi is built on a steep slope above the water, and its defining feature for daily life is stairs: hundreds of them, connecting the coastal road to the old town to the districts above. The promenade running several kilometres along the shore is flat and is how most people move east to west. Buses connect along the coast to Kotor in about an hour, and to Budva and Podgorica beyond. The Kamenari ferry across the mouth of the bay saves a long drive around it. Tivat airport is around 30 minutes by road and Dubrovnik airport in Croatia about 40 minutes, which gives unusually good flight access for a town this size. A car is useful but not essential.
hercegnovi.visas: Montenegro is not in the European Union or the Schengen area, which is the single most useful fact about it for remote workers who have exhausted their Schengen days. Most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, receive 90 days visa-free within a 180-day period. Montenegro introduced a digital nomad residence permit in 2022 for non-EU remote workers employed by or contracting to foreign companies, granting up to two years initially with the possibility of extension, and it came with a publicised tax exemption on foreign income for permit holders. Rules have been refined since launch, so verify the current requirements with a Montenegrin consulate or a local lawyer before relying on older summaries.
hercegnovi.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months. The Bay of Kotor is warm and swimmable from June through September, and Herceg Novi enjoys a notably long growing season, which is why the town is full of mimosa, palms and citrus. July and August are hot and busy, with the coast filling with regional holidaymakers and prices climbing. February brings the Mimosa Festival, the town's signature event, when the tree blooms across the hillside and the town holds weeks of parades. Winter is mild by continental standards, around 12 degrees, but wet: the Bay of Kotor is one of the rainiest places in Europe, and November through January are genuinely soaking.
hercegnovi.prosCons: Herceg Novi sits at the mouth of the Bay of Kotor with mountains behind and Croatia and Dubrovnik airport 40 minutes away, which is a rare combination of scenery and access. It is cheaper than the Croatian coast, uses the euro, offers a long visa-free stay outside Schengen and has a digital nomad permit with a favourable tax position. The old town is genuinely lovely and the swimming season is long. Against that: the stairs are relentless and will not suit anyone with mobility issues. Rainfall is exceptional. The town is small, the nomad community minimal, and healthcare beyond basics means Podgorica. Construction along the coast is aggressive and often ugly, and summer traffic on the single coastal road is severe.
hercegnovi.whoFor: Herceg Novi suits remote workers who want the Adriatic without Schengen days ticking down, who like mountains and sea in the same view, and who are physically comfortable with a town built on a staircase. It works well for anyone on the Montenegrin nomad permit, for people who want Dubrovnik and Kotor within an hour without paying their prices, and for swimmers and hikers. It is a good fit for couples and quiet solo workers. It suits less well anyone who needs a nomad community, dependable dry weather, level ground or serious healthcare nearby. Kotor is more famous and more crowded; Podgorica has the infrastructure; Tivat has the airport and the marina money.

taichung.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,350 a month as a solo remote worker in Taichung, which is meaningfully cheaper than Taipei for a similar standard of urban life. A one-bedroom apartment in the West District or near the Calligraphy Greenway runs about $450 to $650, with the newer Xitun and Nantun districts around the National Taichung Theater costing more and older areas near the railway station considerably less. Groceries land around $300 to $380, though Taiwan's night markets make cooking almost optional. A bowl of beef noodles is $4, a night market dinner $6 to $9, a proper restaurant meal $18 to $28, and bubble tea, which was invented here, about $2. A monthly transit pass is roughly $25. Utilities add $60 to $130, with summer air conditioning dominating.
taichung.whereToWork: Taichung has a healthy coworking scene, concentrated in the West District and Xitun, with desks at roughly $130 to $220 a month and a membership that skews towards Taiwanese startups and designers. The city's real advantage is its cafe density: Taichung takes coffee seriously, and the streets around the Calligraphy Greenway and Shen Ji New Village have an unusual concentration of independent roasters that are entirely comfortable with long laptop sessions. Taiwanese internet is fast, cheap and reliable, both fixed-line and mobile, and public wifi is widespread. English is limited in daily life but common enough in the coworking and startup world, and Taiwanese patience with foreigners attempting Mandarin is considerable.
taichung.gettingAround: Taichung opened its first MRT line in 2021, running north to south through the newer western districts, and it is useful if you live along it and largely irrelevant if you do not. The bus network is extensive and the first ten kilometres of any journey are free with an EasyCard, which is an unusually generous arrangement and the way most residents travel. The city is flat and scooter culture is universal: renting one is the standard solution and transforms daily life. The High Speed Rail station puts Taipei at under an hour and Kaohsiung at 50 minutes, which makes Taichung a genuinely central base. Taichung airport has regional flights; Taoyuan international is about two hours by HSR and shuttle.
taichung.visas: Taiwan grants visa-free entry to most Western passports, typically 90 days for EU, UK, Canadian, Australian and US citizens, and this can often be extended once in-country for a further 90 days, which is more flexible than most. Taiwan launched the Employment Gold Card, a combined work permit, residence visa and re-entry permit valid for one to three years, aimed at qualified professionals across a defined list of fields including technology, finance, education and the arts. It does not require a local employer, which makes it one of the better options in Asia for a self-employed remote worker who qualifies. Applications are made online and processed centrally, and successful holders gain access to Taiwan's excellent national health insurance after six months.
taichung.bestTime: October to April is the comfortable half of the year in Taichung, and the city has a real advantage over Taipei here: it sits in the central plain and gets substantially more sunshine and less rain than the north. Autumn, October and November, is close to ideal, with warm dry days and comfortable nights. Winter is mild, rarely below 12 degrees, and is the season most residents prefer. Spring is pleasant into April. Summer, June to September, is hot and humid, into the mid thirties with high humidity, and is also typhoon season, when storms can close the city for a day or two at a time. The plum rains in May and June bring sustained heavy rainfall.
taichung.prosCons: Taichung is widely considered Taiwan's most liveable city, and the case is strong: better weather than Taipei, lower rents, a flat and scooter-friendly layout, an outstanding food culture, first-class internet and healthcare, and the High Speed Rail putting the whole island within ninety minutes. Taiwan is safe to a degree that surprises most arrivals. Against that, air quality in the central plain is a genuine problem, particularly in winter when it is often the worst in the country. English is limited outside professional circles. The city sprawls and lacks a single obvious centre. The international community is small compared with Taipei, and Taiwan's geopolitical position is a consideration some people weigh heavily.
taichung.whoFor: Taichung suits remote workers who want Asia with excellent infrastructure, genuine safety and world-class food, at a cost well below Tokyo, Singapore or Seoul. It is a strong choice for anyone holding or applying for the Employment Gold Card, for people who intend to learn Mandarin, and for those who want a base with fast rail access to the whole island. Cyclists and hikers do well here, with Sun Moon Lake and the central mountains close. It works for families, given the safety and the healthcare. It suits less well anyone who needs an English-speaking environment, a large expatriate community, or clean air in winter. Taipei has more of the first two and Kaohsiung is warmer and cheaper.

hualien.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,150 a month as a solo remote worker in Hualien, which makes Taiwan's east coast noticeably cheaper than its west. A one-bedroom apartment in Hualien City runs about $350 to $500, and because the city is small and the market is thin, personal contacts and local rental boards often work better than online listings. Groceries land around $280 to $350. Night market food is $4 to $7 a meal, a restaurant dinner $15 to $22, and coffee about $3. A scooter rental is $100 to $150 a month and is close to essential. Utilities add $60 to $120. The main cost variable is travel: Hualien is separated from the west coast by the central mountain range and getting out is a train journey.
hualien.whereToWork: Hualien has essentially no coworking infrastructure, which is the price of its setting. Remote workers here work from their accommodation or from the small but real cluster of independent cafes in the city, several of which have grown up around the surfing and outdoor community and are entirely relaxed about laptops. Taiwanese internet quality holds up here: fixed-line fibre is fast and cheap even in a small east coast city, and mobile 4G and 5G coverage is good along the coastal corridor though patchy in the gorge and the mountains. That reliability is what makes Hualien viable at all as a base. For anything requiring an office or a professional network, Taipei is two hours away by express train.
hualien.gettingAround: Hualien City is small and flat and can be crossed on a bicycle in twenty minutes. Beyond it, a scooter is the standard and near-essential solution: it is how you reach Taroko Gorge, the coastal highway south towards Taitung, and the rice terraces of the East Rift Valley. Rental is cheap and licensing requirements for foreigners should be checked, as enforcement has tightened. Buses run along the main routes but infrequently. The railway is the lifeline to the rest of Taiwan: the Taroko and Puyuma express services reach Taipei in about two hours along a spectacular coastal line, and booking ahead is necessary at weekends and holidays. There is a small airport with limited domestic flights.
hualien.visas: Taiwan grants most Western passports 90 days visa-free on arrival, extendable once in-country for a further 90 days in many cases, which is unusually generous. The Employment Gold Card is the serious long-stay route: a combined open work permit, residence visa and re-entry permit valid for one to three years, aimed at qualified professionals in listed fields and notably not requiring a Taiwanese employer. That makes it one of the most usable schemes in Asia for a self-employed remote worker who meets the criteria. Applications are online and centralised. Holders gain access to Taiwan's national health insurance after six months of residence, which is comprehensive and inexpensive.
hualien.bestTime: October to April is the best window in Hualien. Autumn is warm, clear and dry, and winter is mild at around 15 to 20 degrees, though the east coast is wetter than the west and rain is frequent. Spring through April is pleasant. Summer, June to September, is hot, humid and above all the typhoon season, and this matters more here than anywhere else in Taiwan: Hualien is directly exposed to Pacific storms, and typhoons regularly close Taroko Gorge, cut the coastal highway and cancel trains. The region is also seismically very active, with a major earthquake in April 2024 causing significant damage and landslides in the gorge; check current access before planning around it.
hualien.prosCons: Hualien offers something rare: a small, safe, functional town with Taiwan's infrastructure and healthcare, sitting between the Pacific and the marble walls of Taroko Gorge. The mountains and the coast are genuinely world-class, the food is excellent, internet is fast, and the pace is slow in a way that suits focused work. Costs are low by Taiwanese standards. Against that, it is isolated behind the central range, and the two-hour train to Taipei is the only practical link. There is no nomad or expatriate community. English is very limited. Typhoons and earthquakes are real and recurring disruptions rather than remote possibilities, and the April 2024 quake did serious damage to the gorge road network.
hualien.whoFor: Hualien suits remote workers who want mountains and ocean at the door and are content to supply their own company. It is a strong choice for hikers, climbers, surfers and cyclists, and for anyone on the Employment Gold Card who wants to be somewhere quiet with Taiwanese infrastructure. Writers and people doing deep focused work do well here. It works for couples who like the outdoors. It is a poor fit for anyone needing a professional network, an English-speaking environment, nightlife or a coworking space, and for anyone who would find seismic and typhoon disruption stressful. Taichung and Taipei are both within a few hours and answer all of those far better.

cameronhighlands.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $900 a month as a solo remote worker in the Cameron Highlands, which is inexpensive even by Malaysian standards. A one-bedroom apartment or a room in one of the apartment blocks in Tanah Rata or Brinchang runs about $250 to $400, with older properties cheaper and the small supply of newer builds more. Groceries land around $200 to $270, helped considerably by the fact that this is Malaysia's vegetable garden and produce at the local markets is both excellent and very cheap. A meal at a local restaurant is $3 to $5, a steamboat dinner for two $15 to $20, and a pot of tea at one of the plantations about $4. Utilities are low at $40 to $80: nobody needs air conditioning at 1,500 metres.
cameronhighlands.whereToWork: There is no coworking space in the Cameron Highlands and there is unlikely to be one. Remote workers here work from their accommodation, and the practical question is entirely about connectivity, which is the weak point: fixed-line internet in Tanah Rata is workable but not fast, and speeds vary considerably between buildings and drop in heavy rain, which is frequent. Mobile 4G coverage is reasonable in the main towns and poor in the plantations and on the trails. Anyone whose work depends on video calls should test a specific property's connection before committing. A handful of cafes in Tanah Rata have wifi and are tolerant of laptops, but the town is oriented towards weekend visitors rather than residents.
cameronhighlands.gettingAround: The Cameron Highlands is a string of small towns along a single winding road climbing through the Titiwangsa range: Ringlet, Tanah Rata, Brinchang and Kampung Raja. Tanah Rata is the main base and is walkable end to end in fifteen minutes. Local buses run between the towns cheaply and infrequently, and taxis are available but not plentiful. Most visitors and many residents rent a car or a scooter, which is how you reach the tea estates, the mossy forest and the trailheads. The road up from Tapah or Simpang Pulai is steep and twisting and takes about an hour and a half from the plains. Kuala Lumpur is roughly four hours by bus, Ipoh about two and a half.
cameronhighlands.visas: Malaysia grants most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, 90 days visa-free on arrival, which is generous and covers a substantial stay. For longer, Malaysia runs the DE Rantau Nomad Pass, a purpose-built digital nomad visa for remote workers and freelancers in digital fields, granting up to twelve months with the possibility of a further twelve and allowing dependants. It has an income threshold and requires proof of remote work for foreign clients or employers. Malaysia also operates the Malaysia My Second Home programme, a longer-term residence scheme with substantial financial requirements that has been revised several times. Both are administered nationally rather than locally, so the Highlands present no particular obstacle.
cameronhighlands.bestTime: The Cameron Highlands has no bad season in temperature terms, which is the entire point of the place: at around 1,500 metres it stays between roughly 15 and 25 degrees all year while the Malaysian lowlands sit at 33 and humid. What varies is rain. The drier months are broadly January to March and June to August, and the wettest are October to December, when afternoon downpours are close to daily and can be heavy enough to cause landslides on the access roads. Malaysian school holidays and public holidays fill the towns with domestic visitors and push accommodation prices up sharply, particularly around Chinese New Year and the mid-year break, so a weekday arrival is much cheaper.
cameronhighlands.prosCons: The Cameron Highlands offers something genuinely scarce in Southeast Asia: a cool climate. Sleeping without air conditioning, walking without sweating and hiking in temperate forest are real quality-of-life gains, and they come with very low costs, excellent cheap produce, good hiking and some of the most photogenic agricultural landscape in Asia. Malaysia's visa options are among the region's best. Against that, the internet is the weak link and should not be assumed. The towns are small, functional and not attractive; over-development of the hillsides for farming has done visible damage. There is no community of remote workers, limited healthcare, and getting anywhere means a winding mountain road. Weekends bring heavy domestic tourism.
cameronhighlands.whoFor: The Cameron Highlands suits remote workers who cannot tolerate tropical heat but want tropical costs, and whose work does not depend on a fast, guaranteed connection. It is a strong choice for hikers and for anyone wanting a quiet, cool base to write or study, and it works well as a month or two within a longer Malaysian stay rather than as a permanent home. It is a reasonable escape from Kuala Lumpur or Penang. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs reliable video calls, a social scene, nightlife, good healthcare nearby or an airport within reach. Penang and Kuala Lumpur have all of that, at higher cost and in far more heat.

quetzaltenango.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Quetzaltenango, which makes it one of the cheapest bases in Latin America. A one-bedroom apartment in Zona 1 near the central park or in the quieter Zona 3 runs about $220 to $350, and rooms in shared houses, common because of the language schools, go for $120 to $200. Groceries land around $150 to $200, with the Minerva and Democracia markets far cheaper than supermarkets. A comedor lunch is $2.50 to $4, a restaurant dinner $8 to $14, and coffee, which Guatemala grows superbly, about $1.50. A week of one-to-one Spanish tuition, twenty hours, typically costs $100 to $150 including a homestay, which is the reason many people come.
quetzaltenango.whereToWork: Xela, as everyone calls it, has a small coworking presence and a much larger cafe culture built around its long-established Spanish school industry and a sizeable population of long-term foreign students and NGO workers. Cafes around the central park and in Zona 1 are used to laptops and long stays. Coworking, where it exists, runs about $70 to $120 a month. Connectivity is the thing to check: fibre has reached parts of the city and is genuinely fast, while older buildings can be poor, and power cuts are not rare. Mobile data is cheap and coverage is reliable. Xela sits at 2,330 metres, which affects nothing about work and a great deal about how you feel in the first week.
quetzaltenango.gettingAround: Quetzaltenango is compact and its centre is walkable, though the altitude and the hills make it more tiring than the map suggests. Local buses and shared microbuses cover the wider city for well under a dollar and are crowded and quick. Taxis and ride-hailing apps are cheap and widely used, particularly at night. For getting out, the second-class chicken buses are an experience and go everywhere in the western highlands, while shuttle services aimed at travellers run comfortably to Antigua, Lake Atitlán and the Mexican border. Guatemala City and its international airport are about four hours away by road. A car is not necessary and driving in the highlands at night is generally discouraged.
quetzaltenango.visas: Guatemala is part of the CA-4 agreement with El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua, which functions as a shared 90-day zone: most Western passports get 90 days on arrival, but that allowance covers all four countries together, so a border run to El Salvador does not reset it. Extensions of a further 90 days can be applied for once at the immigration office in Guatemala City. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays generally require residency, most commonly through the pensionado route for those with a qualifying pension, through investment, or through marriage. Many long-term foreign residents in Xela simply cycle out to Mexico or Belize, which does reset the CA-4 clock, and this is a well-worn if imperfect practice.
quetzaltenango.bestTime: November to April is the dry season and the best time in Xela, with bright clear days, cold nights and the volcanoes visible. The altitude means it is never hot: daytime highs sit around 20 to 22 degrees year-round and nights drop close to freezing in December and January, so heating, which few buildings have, becomes a real consideration. The wet season runs May to October, with rain concentrated in heavy afternoon downpours rather than all-day drizzle, and mornings usually clear; September and October are the wettest and carry some risk of landslides on highland roads. Semana Santa in the week before Easter is spectacular across Guatemala and fills every bed in the country.
quetzaltenango.prosCons: Xela is cheap, genuinely Guatemalan rather than a traveller enclave, and the best place in the country to learn Spanish properly, with dozens of long-established schools and homestays at prices that seem implausible from Europe. It sits in the western highlands with volcanoes, hot springs and Maya market towns all around, and it has a real university and an intellectual life. Against that, the altitude is high enough to need acclimatising, nights are cold in unheated buildings, and the rainy season is wet. Infrastructure is patchy: power and water interruptions happen. Personal security requires the ordinary Latin American caution, particularly at night. There is no nomad scene as such, and the foreign population is students and NGO workers.
quetzaltenango.whoFor: Quetzaltenango suits remote workers who want to learn Spanish seriously and live very cheaply while doing it, and who prefer a working highland city to a traveller town. It is a strong choice for anyone interested in Maya culture and the western highlands, for volunteers and NGO people, and for those who want Guatemala without Antigua's prices and tourism. It works well for solo travellers, given the ready-made community around the language schools. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs guaranteed power and internet, warm weather, a beach, a nomad crowd or an airport nearby. Antigua is the obvious alternative: prettier, more expensive, far more foreign, and four hours closer to the airport.

puertoviejo.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in Puerto Viejo, which reflects the general truth that Costa Rica is not cheap by Central American standards. A one-bedroom place in town or in the surrounding jungle runs about $600 to $900 on a long lease, with beachfront and newer builds well above that, and short-term rates in high season considerably higher again. Groceries land around $350 to $450, with imported goods expensive and the local ferias good value for produce. A casado lunch at a soda is $6 to $9, a restaurant dinner $18 to $30, and a beer about $3. A scooter or bicycle is the standard local transport. Utilities add $80 to $150, largely fans and refrigeration.
puertoviejo.whereToWork: Puerto Viejo has no formal coworking space, and remote workers here work from their accommodation or from the town's cafes, several of which have grown up specifically around the surfing and long-stay crowd and are entirely comfortable with laptops. The constraint is connectivity: this is the Caribbean coast, infrastructure is thinner than in the Central Valley, and fixed-line speeds vary sharply by property. Anyone dependent on video calls should test the actual connection before committing to a lease, and should budget for a mobile data backup, as 4G coverage in town is reasonable. Power cuts happen, particularly in the wet season. Many long-stayers keep a small battery backup for the router as a matter of course.
puertoviejo.gettingAround: Puerto Viejo is a small town and the standard way to move is a bicycle: the coastal road running south through Playa Cocles, Chiquita and Punta Uva to Manzanillo is flat, shaded and lined with the beaches most people come for, and cycling it is a large part of the appeal. Scooters are common. Buses run along the coast and north to Limón and on to San José, a journey of about four and a half hours to the capital. There is no airport nearby; San José's Juan Santamaría is the international gateway, and the domestic strip at Limón has limited service.
